title: RiskEngine Methodology Notes
text:
Author: Owen Gallagher, Head of Risk
Last updated: 2026-07-03
Owner team: Risk
Audience: Risk, Trading, Wealth Management, Operations, Compliance, Technology

Purpose
These notes describe how RiskEngine produces intraday Value at Risk (VaR) and exposure figures, which inputs it relies on, and where the numbers surface in ReportingBI. They are meant to help desk heads, analysts and engineers interpret the outputs correctly and know who to contact when something looks off. No client-level data is reproduced here; where a client needs to be discussed, use the client reference id in ClientHub.

Scope and Upstream Dependencies
RiskEngine is a critical system owned by Risk. It consumes two upstream feeds: prices and valuations from PricingSvc, and holdings from PositionStore. PricingSvc in turn depends on MarketDataFeed, so a stale exchange or vendor feed will eventually show up as stale risk. If either PricingSvc or PositionStore is degraded, RiskEngine flags the affected run as partial rather than silently using old data.

VaR Approach
The primary measure is one-day historical simulation VaR at 99% confidence, using a rolling window of 500 business days of risk-factor returns. Returns are absolute for rates and spreads, and relative for equities, FX and commodities. Scenarios are equally weighted. We do not apply decay weighting in the headline number, though a 94% exponentially weighted variant is calculated alongside it as a sensitivity and is available to Paul Hansen and the market risk team on request.

We also report 95% VaR and expected shortfall at 97.5%. Expected shortfall is the figure we look at first when the desk has concentrated or option-heavy books, because VaR alone understates tail behavior there.

Run Cadence
Full revaluation runs happen at the start of day, using the prior close snapshot from PositionStore. Intraday refreshes run every 15 minutes between market open and close. Intraday runs use delta-gamma approximations for option positions and full revaluation only for the top positions by notional. The end-of-day run uses full revaluation for everything and is the version that feeds regulatory and management reporting.

Exposure Measures
Beyond VaR, RiskEngine publishes gross and net exposure by desk, by asset class and by issuer. Single-issuer concentration is measured against the limit framework approved by the risk committee. Counterparty exposure is calculated as current mark-to-market plus a simple add-on by product type; Credit Risk (Lance Peters, Phillip Jackson, John Garcia) owns the add-on table and reviews it quarterly.

Limits and Escalation
Desk VaR limits are set by Risk with input from Daniel Reyes for Trading. A breach is defined as the intraday 99% VaR exceeding the limit on two consecutive refreshes. A single-refresh excursion is logged but not escalated unless it exceeds 120% of limit. Escalation path:
1. Market Risk (Paul Hansen) contacts the desk head.
2. If unresolved within 30 minutes, Owen Gallagher is informed.
3. Persistent breaches are reported to Martin Osei and noted in the daily risk summary.

Backtesting
We compare daily P&L against the prior day's 99% VaR. Exceptions are counted over a trailing 250 business days. Four or fewer exceptions is green, five to nine is amber, ten or more is red. Each exception is documented with cause: market move, position change after the snapshot, or model or data issue. Amber and red results are reviewed with Compliance before being included in regulatory reporting.

Known Limitations
Intraday delta-gamma approximation can understate risk in large moves for barrier and short-dated options. Illiquid instruments use proxy series, which dampens measured volatility. Positions booked after the snapshot are not reflected until the next intraday refresh. Wealth Management portfolios in PortfolioMgr are covered at an aggregated level and are not part of desk VaR.

Reporting in ReportingBI
ReportingBI reads RiskEngine output together with GLCore and DataLake. The risk dashboards display the end-of-day figures, not the latest intraday refresh, unless the tile is labeled intraday. If a dashboard number differs from the RiskEngine console, check the run timestamp first, then whether the run was marked partial.

Change Control
Any change to the window length, confidence level, scenario weighting or proxy mapping requires model validation sign-off from Risk and notice to Trading and Operations at least five business days before release. Engineering changes to the service itself go through the standard release process with Technology, and Sam Okafor's team is the contact for deployment questions.

Contacts
Methodology questions: Owen Gallagher
Market risk and limits: Paul Hansen
Credit exposure add-ons: Lance Peters
Platform issues: post in #it-ops; incidents go to #incidents
General risk questions: #risk

title: Disaster Recovery Test Results (July)
text:
Disaster Recovery Test Results (July)
Author: Sam Okafor, Director of Engineering
Last updated: 2026-07-07

Purpose and Scope
This report summarizes the July disaster recovery exercise, run on Saturday 2026-07-04 between 06:00 and 12:30 ET. The goal was to validate failover of the trading-critical path from the primary data center to the secondary site and confirm we still meet our recovery targets of 30 minutes RTO and 5 minutes RPO for critical systems. The focus this cycle was OMS and PricingSvc, along with the upstream and downstream pieces they need to function: MarketDataFeed, AuthSSO, and TradeBlotter.

Test Design
We failed over in dependency order. AuthSSO went first because OMS depends on it for session authentication. MarketDataFeed and PricingSvc followed, since PricingSvc consumes the feed and OMS depends on PricingSvc for pre-trade valuation and limit checks. OMS was brought up last, then TradeBlotter. Omar Brown and Barbara Beard ran the SRE runbooks. Leo Martinez monitored replication lag on the Technology side. Daniel Reyes nominated Steven Farley and Jonathan Mcdonald from the desk to run synthetic order flow after failover. Ravi Patel observed for Operations.

Results Summary
AuthSSO: failover completed in 7 minutes. Passed.
MarketDataFeed: vendor and exchange connections re-established at the secondary site in 14 minutes. Passed, with one note below.
PricingSvc: recovered in 11 minutes after the feed was stable, with cache warm-up finishing at 19 minutes. Passed.
OMS: recovered in 24 minutes from the start of the exercise to accepting orders. Passed, but with only 6 minutes of margin against the 30 minute target.
TradeBlotter: recovered in 27 minutes. Passed.
Measured RPO for OMS was under 2 minutes. Measured RPO for PricingSvc reference data was under 1 minute.

What Went Well
The AuthSSO failover was the cleanest it has been. The scripted DNS cutover removed the manual step that caused delays in the January test. Synthetic order flow of about 400 test orders passed pre-trade checks with valuations matching primary-site results within tolerance. No orders were lost or duplicated during the cutover.

Issues Found
1. OMS recovery time. The OMS startup waited on PricingSvc health checks with a conservative timeout, adding roughly 6 minutes of idle time. This is the main reason the margin is thin. We will tune the retry and backoff settings and validate them in the August tabletop.
2. MarketDataFeed entitlements. One vendor connection required a manual entitlement refresh at the secondary site, which cost about 5 minutes. The vendor has confirmed that site-based entitlements can be pre-provisioned. Owner: Technology.
3. PricingSvc cache warm-up. Until the cache was fully warm, the first valuations for illiquid instruments returned slowly. Desk users saw delays of up to 8 seconds on some quotes. This was within tolerance for the test but would be noticeable in a live trading session.
4. Runbook drift. Two steps in the OMS runbook referenced hostnames that were retired in the spring. SRE corrected them during the exercise and the updated runbook is now in the wiki.

Dependencies Not Tested
SettlementEngine, which depends on OMS and GLCore, was not part of this exercise. Operations will need to confirm downstream settlement behavior in a separate test, since a failed-over OMS feeds it. RiskEngine, which depends on PricingSvc and PositionStore, was only spot-checked, and Owen Gallagher's team has asked for a full run in the next cycle.

Feedback From the Desk
Daniel Reyes reported that the desk was comfortable with the recovered OMS but wants a clearer status banner during failover so traders know when pre-trade checks are fully live. We have logged this as an enhancement for the OMS team.

Action Items
Tune OMS startup health check timeouts. Owner: Leo Martinez. Due 2026-07-31.
Pre-provision vendor entitlements at the secondary site. Owner: Omar Brown. Due 2026-08-14.
Add a PricingSvc cache pre-warm step to the failover runbook. Owner: Barbara Beard. Due 2026-07-24.
Coordinate a combined OMS and SettlementEngine failover test with Operations. Owner: Sam Okafor with Ravi Patel. Target: September.
Include RiskEngine in the full failover sequence. Owner: Technology with Risk. Target: September.

Conclusion
All five systems in scope met their recovery targets, and no data loss was observed. The thin OMS margin is the key concern and is being addressed first. We will report progress on the action items in the next monthly Technology operations review.

title: ReconLegacy Runbook (v3.2)
text:
ReconLegacy Runbook (v3.2)
Owner: Technology. Last updated Fri 2026-07-10 by Priya Raman.

Purpose
ReconLegacy is the end-of-day reconciliation batch. It matches settled trades from SettlementEngine against GLCore balances and publishes a break report to #recon for the Operations reconciliation team. It is a set of Perl batch jobs on a single Oracle 11g host (reconprd01). It is a legacy system. Treat changes conservatively and test against the UAT schema first.

Schedule
The master wrapper (recon_master.pl) runs from cron at 02:15 ET, Monday through Saturday. The Saturday run covers Friday activity. Normal completion is between 04:45 and 05:30. The break report must be posted to #recon by 06:30 ET. If it has not posted by 06:00, start triage.

Job Steps
Step 1, load_settle.pl: picks up the SettlementEngine extract files from the inbound SFTP drop. Expects the trade file and the cash movements file, both stamped with the business date.
Step 2, load_gl.pl: pulls GLCore end-of-day balances through the read-only DB link.
Step 3, match_core.pl: runs the matching rules (trade ref, CUSIP/ISIN, quantity, net amount tolerance) and writes into RECON.BREAK_HIST.
Step 4, load_fx.pl: loads the FX rate table from the PricingSvc end-of-day snapshot. It then re-values non-USD legs and re-runs the match for those legs.
Step 5, publish.pl: renders the break report and posts it to #recon through the webhook. It also archives a CSV to the shared recon folder.

Each step writes to /var/log/recon/<step>_<YYYYMMDD>.log and records its status in RECON.JOB_STATUS.

Common Failures

1. Late settlement file
Symptom: step 1 log shows "waiting for settle extract". After 90 minutes it exits with RC=12.
Action: confirm with Operations (Settlements) that SettlementEngine has finished its EOD run. Once the files land, restart from step 1:
  recon_master.pl --from-step 1
If the files are for the right date but the names are wrong, do not rename them by hand. Escalate to the SettlementEngine on-call.

2. Oracle tablespace full (ORA-01653)
Symptom: step 3 aborts with "ORA-01653: unable to extend table RECON.BREAK_HIST". This usually happens after high-volume days or at quarter end.
Action: check free space in RECON_DATA with the dba_free_space query in scripts/space_check.sql. Add a datafile or resize the existing one, following the DBA standard in the Oracle wiki. Do not enable autoextend without a max size. Then restart from step 3:
  recon_master.pl --from-step 3
If space is fine, purge BREAK_HIST partitions older than 13 months using purge_hist.pl. That is the retention policy agreed with Compliance.

3. FX rate table not loaded from the PricingSvc snapshot
Symptom: the report shows a cluster of breaks, all on FX or non-USD trades, with amount differences that look like a rate mismatch. The step 4 log shows "snapshot not found" or a snapshot timestamp from the prior day.
Action: confirm that the PricingSvc EOD snapshot has published. PricingSvc depends on MarketDataFeed, so check #incidents for feed issues first. Then re-run step 4 only:
  recon_master.pl --step 4
and re-publish:
  recon_master.pl --step 5
Step 4 has a stale-price guard. If the snapshot is older than the business date, the job aborts on purpose instead of valuing breaks at old rates.

Re-running a Prior Business Date
Use the --asof flag, for example:
  recon_master.pl --asof 2026-07-09
This reloads that date's inputs and overwrites that date's rows in BREAK_HIST. Tell #recon before you run it, because analysts may already be working those breaks.

Not Covered in This Runbook
The FX adjustment module (fx_adj.pm, called inside step 4) and the month-end manual override process are not documented here. Both rely on hand-maintained config and on judgment calls made at month end. Do not change either without talking to me first.

Contacts
Primary: Priya Raman (Technology)
Business users: Tasha Greene, Reconciliation (Operations)
Escalation: Sam Okafor, Director of Engineering

title: Settlement Fails Playbook
text:
Settlement Fails Playbook
Owner: Ravi Patel, Head of Operations
Last updated: 2026-07-14
Applies to: Operations (Settlements, Payments, Wire Room), Trading, Risk, Compliance

Purpose
This playbook describes how Halcyon Ridge Capital identifies, triages, escalates, and resolves failed settlements. A fail is any trade that does not settle on its contractual settlement date because of missing securities, missing cash, instruction mismatch, or a counterparty or custodian issue. The goal is to cut aged fails, limit financing and buy-in costs, and keep Trading, Risk, and Finance informed early.

Systems Involved
SettlementEngine is the system of record for trade settlement and clearing. All fails are tracked there as exceptions with a status, reason code, and age in business days. PaymentsGateway handles ACH and wire cash movements, and is the route for cash funding of fails and for claims and compensation payments. SettlementEngine depends on OMS and GLCore, so a fail can originate from an upstream order or ledger problem as well as from the counterparty. Before escalating externally, always confirm that OMS trade details and GLCore postings are correct.

Daily Fails Routine
1. By 07:30 ET the Settlements Specialist on shift pulls the overnight exceptions report from SettlementEngine and tags every item with a reason code: SHORT (securities not delivered), CASH (funding shortfall), MISMATCH (instruction or SSI discrepancy), CPTY (counterparty or custodian hold), or INTERNAL (booking or allocation error).
2. By 08:15 ET the settlements lead posts the fails summary in #recon with counts by reason code, aggregate notional, and any item aged three business days or more.
3. Items tagged INTERNAL are routed immediately to the owning desk. Trading must confirm or amend allocations in OMS by 09:30 ET.
4. Items tagged MISMATCH are re-confirmed with the counterparty and the instruction is corrected and resubmitted the same morning.
5. By 14:00 ET the team reviews all open items against the cut-offs of the custodians and clearing agents so that remaining fixes can still land for same-day settlement.

Cash Funding and Wire Handling
When a fail is caused by a cash shortfall, the Settlements Specialist requests funding through the Payments team. Any wire release goes through PaymentsGateway and is processed by the Wire Room under standard dual approval. No one may release a payment they initiated. The Wire Room console shows the status, but the payment record in PaymentsGateway is authoritative. If a payment is held by fraud scoring, do not work around the hold. Contact Compliance in #compliance and wait for clearance.

Escalation Thresholds
Age one business day: Settlements owns the item and contacts the counterparty operations desk.
Age three business days: Escalate to the Head of Operations and notify the responsible Trading desk head. Trading must provide a view on whether to cancel and rebook, borrow securities, or wait.
Age five business days, or any single fail above $5M notional: Notify Risk, specifically the Market Risk Manager, who assesses exposure and capital impact. Finance is copied so that financing charges can be accrued in GLCore.
Any fail exposed to a mandatory buy-in: Escalate the same day to the Head of Operations and the Chief Operating Officer. Trading decides on action before the buy-in notice deadline.

Resolution Options
Partial settlement where the counterparty and custodian permit it, which reduces exposure quickly.
Securities borrow or a sourced delivery through the Trading desk.
Cancel and rebook for genuine booking errors, only with Trading and Compliance agreement where the change affects a reportable record.
Claims and compensation for costs caused by the counterparty, documented in SettlementEngine and paid or received through PaymentsGateway.

Incident Handling
If more than ten fails share a common cause, such as a SettlementEngine outage or a stale feed from OMS, treat it as an operational incident. Open a thread in #incidents, name an incident lead from Operations, and notify Technology through #it-ops. Settlements must keep a manual log of affected trades until the system is confirmed healthy. Note that ReconLegacy, the legacy end-of-day reconciliation batch, will show breaks for fails. Do not clear these breaks manually until the underlying fail is resolved or formally written off.

Documentation and Reporting
Every fail needs a note in SettlementEngine with the reason code, counterparty contact, actions taken, and expected settlement date. The weekly fails report goes to the Chief Operating Officer and the Head of Risk every Monday and includes aging buckets, repeat counterparties, and total financing cost. Counterparties that cause repeated fails are reviewed monthly with Trading and Risk.

Questions
Post in #recon or contact Ravi Patel directly. This playbook is reviewed each quarter and after any significant fail event.

title: Information Barrier and MNPI Policy
text:
Information Barrier and MNPI Policy
Effective: Wednesday, July 15, 2026
Owner: Marcus Bell, Chief Compliance Officer
Applies to: All Halcyon Ridge Capital employees, contractors and temporary staff

Purpose
Halcyon Ridge runs advisory, lending, wealth and trading businesses under one roof. This policy sets out how we keep material non-public information (MNPI) inside the people who need it, so that we protect our clients, our counterparties and the firm's licenses. If you are unsure whether something is covered, assume it is and call the Control Room.

What Counts as MNPI
Information is material if a reasonable investor would consider it important to a decision to buy, sell or hold a security, or if it would likely move the price. It is non-public until it has been broadly disseminated, for example through a press release or regulatory filing, and the market has had time to absorb it. Typical examples include pending mergers, acquisitions, tender offers or divestitures; unannounced earnings or guidance; significant financing, restructuring or credit events; major customer wins or losses; senior management changes; and material litigation or labor actions. Valuation ranges, bid levels, deal timing and the identity of parties in a live mandate are always MNPI.

Deal Codenames
Every advisory mandate receives a codename from the Control Room at engagement. Codenames must be used in all internal communications, calendar invites, file names and system entries. Do not pair a codename with a ticker, company name or obvious descriptor outside the approved deal-team channel or data room.

Wall-Crossing Procedure
No one may be brought over the wall without prior Control Room approval. The deal lead submits a wall-crossing request naming the individual, the business reason and the expected duration. Compliance reviews for conflicts, including outside brokerage accounts and recent personal trading, and records the approval. The crossed individual receives a written acknowledgment that they now hold MNPI and must not trade in, recommend or discuss the affected securities. Wall crossings are logged and reviewed monthly; the deal lead must notify the Control Room when a person no longer needs access.

Restricted and Watch Lists
The Watch List is confidential to Compliance and lists issuers about which the firm may hold MNPI; it is used for surveillance and is never distributed. The Restricted List is circulated firm-wide and prohibits proprietary trading, solicited client trading, research commentary and personal trading in listed issuers. Additions are made by the Control Room and are effective immediately. OMS pre-trade controls block restricted names; overrides require written Compliance sign-off.

Where Deal Discussion Is Allowed
Live transactions may only be discussed in the private, Compliance-administered deal-team channel for that codename, in the approved virtual data room, and on calls or in meetings limited to wall-crossed staff. Deal discussion is prohibited in public channels such as #general, #trading-desk, #random or #ma-team, in direct messages with anyone not crossed, and in elevators, the cafeteria or any public setting. Personal email and messaging apps may never be used.

Trading Desk Separation
Traders, sales traders, quant analysts and trading associates must never receive MNPI. Advisory staff must not take calls from, share screens with or sit with Trading personnel on deal matters. If a trader believes they have inadvertently received MNPI, they must stop all activity in the relevant name, tell no one else, and contact the Control Room immediately.

Escalation
Report suspected leaks, unauthorized access or accidental disclosure to Marcus Bell or the Compliance team in #compliance with no deal details, or by phone. Compliance will assess whether the issuer should be restricted and whether a broader review is required. Good-faith reporting is protected from retaliation.

Disciplinary Consequences
Breaches of this policy may result in disciplinary action up to and including termination, clawback of compensation, and referral to regulators and law enforcement. Insider trading and tipping carry personal civil and criminal liability. Managers who fail to supervise are accountable as well.

Questions
Direct questions to the Control Room. This policy is reviewed annually.

title: Q3 2026 Compliance Testing Report
text:
Q3 2026 Compliance Testing Report
Author: Marcus Bell, Chief Compliance Officer
Last updated: 2026-07-15
Status: Interim, covers the first two weeks of Q3 and the approved test plan for the remainder of the quarter

Purpose and Scope
This report summarizes the compliance testing program for Q3 2026 across KYC/CDD onboarding, sanctions screening, AML transaction monitoring, fraud scoring, and suspicious activity reporting. It also sets out the sampling approach, early findings, and open remediation items. Testing is performed by the Compliance team, with data pulls supported by Technology and process walkthroughs supported by Operations, Lending, and Wealth Management.

Systems in Scope
KYCPipeline, SanctionsScreen, AMLMonitor, FraudScore, SARFiling, and PaymentsGateway controls. We also test upstream dependencies where a failure would silently weaken a control: DataLake (feeds both FraudScore and AMLMonitor), DocVault and ClientHub (inputs to KYCPipeline), and AuthSSO (access control for the above).

Test Plan Summary
1. KYC/CDD file review. Nadia Petrov's team and the KYC specialists, John Smith and Luis Bowen, will sample onboarding files from Wealth Management and Lending each month, checking beneficial ownership capture, document completeness in DocVault, risk rating rationale, and timeliness of periodic reviews.
2. Sanctions screening effectiveness. Anthony Ramirez will run a controlled test set of synthetic name variations (transliterations, truncations, reordered fields) through SanctionsScreen to confirm match thresholds and list refresh timing.
3. AML monitoring scenario tuning. Daniel Sanchez and Heather Carlson will review alert-to-case conversion rates for each AMLMonitor scenario and back-test thresholds against the prior two quarters of data.
4. Fraud scoring and wire controls. Jenna Cho will validate that FraudScore decisions are reaching PaymentsGateway before release, and that WireRoom operators cannot bypass held items without a documented override.
5. SAR timeliness. Linda Jones will test SARFiling case aging against the regulatory filing deadlines and confirm supporting documents are attached from DocVault.
6. Access recertification. Quarterly review of privileged access to the in-scope systems, reconciled against AuthSSO group membership and HRIS records.

Early Results (July 1 to July 15)
Sanctions screening: The initial synthetic test set returned the expected matches for exact and near-exact variants. Two transliteration patterns scored just below the review threshold. We have asked Jenna Cho to document the current fuzzy-match settings and to propose a threshold change for approval before any production adjustment.

KYC files: The first sample from Wealth Management showed generally strong documentation. The main exception theme is stale periodic reviews, where the review date passed without a refreshed risk rating. Lending files showed a few cases where the KYC clearance record was not linked to the loan file in LoanOrigination. Brian Kowalski has been informed and will assign follow-up to the Lending relationship managers.

AML monitoring: Alert volumes are stable. One scenario covering rapid movement of funds shows a low conversion rate to cases and is a candidate for tuning. No changes will be made until back-testing is complete.

Fraud and payments: Initial walkthroughs with Ravi Patel's team confirmed that held wires are logged with approver identity. We are still validating the behavior during a FraudScore degradation event, since PaymentsGateway depends on it. A tabletop exercise is scheduled with Operations and Technology.

Open Items and Dependencies
KYCPipeline ownership moves from Operations to Compliance on 2026-10-06. We will use Q3 testing results as the baseline for that handover and will ask Operations to confirm all open pipeline exceptions and runbooks are documented before the transition. Testing of KYCPipeline will continue through the changeover so the evidence trail is unbroken.

We also need a confirmed data retention and lineage description for DataLake feeds into AMLMonitor and FraudScore. Sam Okafor has agreed to provide this from Technology by the end of August.

Risk Ratings and Escalation
Current overall assessment is moderate. The threshold tuning on sanctions matching and the stale periodic reviews are rated medium. No high-severity findings are open. Any finding that suggests a reportable breach will be escalated to me immediately and to Catherine Hale and Owen Gallagher the same day.

Next Steps
Complete the second KYC sampling round by the end of August. Finish AMLMonitor back-testing by mid-September. Hold the FraudScore degradation tabletop in August. Issue the final Q3 report by 2026-10-16, ahead of the October handover period closing out.

Questions can be sent to me directly or raised in #compliance.

Marcus Bell
Chief Compliance Officer

title: Access Management Standard
text:
Access Management Standard
Owner: Barbara Beard, Site Reliability Engineer, Technology
Last updated: 2026-07-21
Applies to: All Halcyon Ridge Capital employees, contractors, and service accounts

Purpose
This standard defines how access to Halcyon Ridge production systems is requested, approved, granted, reviewed, and removed. It exists to enforce least privilege, keep a clear audit trail for regulators and internal audit, and reduce the blast radius of any compromised credential. It is maintained by Technology Site Reliability Engineering in coordination with Compliance and Risk.

Scope
The standard covers all production and production-adjacent systems, with particular emphasis on those classed as critical. Two systems are called out here because they have distinct access patterns: MarketDataFeed, which ingests real-time exchange and vendor data, and ReconLegacy, the legacy end-of-day reconciliation batch running Perl on Oracle 11g. Other systems follow the same baseline rules unless a system-specific addendum says otherwise.

Core Principles
1. Least privilege: users receive only the access needed for their current role.
2. Role-based access first: access is granted through AuthSSO groups mapped to job function, not by individual entitlements, wherever possible.
3. Separation of duties: no individual may both request and approve the same access, and no one person may both deploy and approve a production change to a critical system.
4. Individual accountability: shared accounts are prohibited except for documented break-glass credentials.

Requesting Access
All requests are raised in the IT access ticket queue and must state the system, the access level, the business justification, and the requested duration. The requester's manager approves the business need. The system owner team approves the technical entitlement. For critical systems, a second approval from the owning team lead is required. Requests for access that touches regulated data, such as client records in DocVault or KYC screening results, also require Compliance sign-off.

System-Specific Requirements
MarketDataFeed: Read access to market data outputs is available to Trading, Risk, and Quant users through their standard role groups. Write or configuration access to ingestion handlers, vendor credentials, and exchange connectivity settings is restricted to Technology engineers on the MarketDataFeed rota. Changes to vendor entitlements must be recorded so that exchange licensing and usage reporting remain accurate. Because PricingSvc depends on MarketDataFeed, any elevated access during market hours requires an approved change record and an SRE on standby.

ReconLegacy: Because the Oracle 11g database does not integrate natively with AuthSSO, access is managed through named database accounts that are provisioned manually by Technology and recorded in the access register. Operations Reconciliation users receive read-only access for break investigation. Write access to batch schedules, Perl scripts, or database objects is limited to a small group of named Technology engineers and is granted for a fixed window only. Passwords for these accounts are vaulted and rotated every 90 days. Any new access to ReconLegacy must be reviewed by the Head of Operations, since the batch depends on SettlementEngine and GLCore outputs.

Privileged and Emergency Access
Privileged access is time-bound and expires automatically, with a maximum of 8 hours for production sessions. Break-glass access may be used during a declared incident in #incidents. The incident commander must approve its use, all sessions are recorded, and the credential is rotated within one business day. A post-use review is completed by SRE and shared with Compliance.

Access Reviews
System owners perform quarterly recertification of all access to critical systems and semi-annual recertification for standard and legacy systems. Reviewers must explicitly confirm or revoke each entitlement; silence is not approval. Unreviewed entitlements are removed after a 10 business day grace period. Compliance spot-checks a sample of reviews each quarter, and findings are reported to the Chief Compliance Officer and the Head of Risk.

Joiners, Movers, and Leavers
New joiners receive role-based baseline access on their start date. Movers have prior-team access removed within 5 business days of the transfer date, and managers are responsible for raising the removal ticket. For leavers, HR triggers deprovisioning through HRIS, and AuthSSO accounts must be disabled by close of business on the last working day. Manually managed accounts, including those on ReconLegacy, are removed by Technology on the same day, and any shared secrets the leaver knew are rotated. Where a departing employee owns systems or runbooks, the owning manager must name a successor before the last day.

Logging and Monitoring
All authentication events and privileged commands are forwarded to DataLake for retention and analysis. Alerts for anomalous access, such as off-hours privileged logins or repeated failures, route to the Technology on-call and to Compliance.

Exceptions
Exceptions require written justification, a compensating control, and approval from the Director of Engineering and the Chief Compliance Officer. Exceptions expire after 90 days and must be renewed explicitly.

Questions
Raise questions in #it-ops or contact Barbara Beard in Technology SRE.

title: Wealth Model Portfolio Guide
text:
Wealth Model Portfolio Guide
Owner: Grace Lin, Head of Wealth Management
Last updated: 2026-07-27

Purpose
This guide explains how the Wealth Management team builds, assigns, monitors, and rebalances model portfolios for advisory clients. It is meant for advisors, portfolio managers, relationship managers, and client associates. It does not cover discretionary mandates negotiated bespoke with a client; those follow the separate investment policy statement process.

Model Lineup
We maintain five core models, each with a stated risk band, a strategic asset allocation, and tolerance bands around each sleeve:

1. Capital Preservation: short-duration Treasuries, investment-grade credit, and a small equity sleeve.
2. Income: laddered municipal and corporate bonds, dividend equity, and a modest alternatives allocation.
3. Balanced: roughly 60/40 equity to fixed income with global diversification.
4. Growth: equity-heavy with factor tilts and a capped satellite allocation.
5. Opportunistic Growth: highest equity weight, available only to clients whose profile supports it.

Portfolio managers Janet Brown, Tricia Kelly, and Michael Castillo each own specific models and are accountable for construction, security selection, and commentary. Model ownership is listed in PortfolioMgr on each model's header record.

Assigning a Client to a Model
Suitability comes first. The advisor or relationship manager completes the risk profile, time horizon, liquidity needs, and any restrictions in ClientHub. The profile must be current, meaning refreshed within the last 12 months or after any material life event the client reports. Once the profile is complete:

1. The advisor proposes a model in ClientHub with a short written rationale.
2. A senior advisor, typically Jamie Washington, reviews any case where the proposed model is more than one step away from the risk score output.
3. The client associate records the signed investment agreement in ClientHub and confirms the model assignment.
4. The assignment is then mirrored in PortfolioMgr, where the account is linked to the model and any client-specific restrictions are entered as overlays.

Never assign a model in PortfolioMgr until the ClientHub profile and signed agreement are both on file. If the two systems disagree, ClientHub is the source of truth for suitability and PortfolioMgr is the source of truth for holdings and targets.

Restrictions and Overlays
Common overlays include excluded sectors or issuers, concentrated legacy positions with tax sensitivity, and cash raise requests. Overlays are entered as account-level exceptions in PortfolioMgr, and each needs an expiry or review date. The portfolio manager approves any overlay that moves an account more than 3 percentage points from model weights in a single sleeve.

Rebalancing
PortfolioMgr runs a drift check each trading day after pricing is refreshed. Accounts breach the trigger when any sleeve is outside its tolerance band, typically plus or minus 4 percent of the target weight, or when cash falls below the model minimum. In addition, we conduct a full calendar rebalance each quarter.

The process is:

1. The portfolio manager reviews the drift report and the proposed trade list generated by PortfolioMgr.
2. Tax-aware adjustments are applied: harvest losses where appropriate, avoid short-term gains where possible, and respect wash sale windows.
3. Approved trades are released to the trading desk in blocks. Wealth does not route orders directly; the desk handles execution.
4. After settlement, the client associate confirms holdings in PortfolioMgr and notes the rebalance in the ClientHub activity log.

If pricing looks stale or PortfolioMgr shows missing prices, pause rebalancing and raise it in #it-ops. PortfolioMgr depends on PricingSvc and PositionStore, so a problem in either can produce bad drift numbers.

Model Changes
When a portfolio manager changes a model's allocation or swaps a holding, the change is documented with a rationale, expected turnover, and tax impact estimate. Changes affecting more than 10 percent of a model's weights need my sign-off. Advisors should receive written notice before the changes reach client accounts so they can answer questions. Clients on a model are communicated with through the relationship manager, and every outreach is logged in ClientHub.

Monitoring and Reporting
Portfolio managers review performance against the model benchmark monthly and present results at the Wealth team meeting. Accounts lagging their model by more than 75 basis points over a rolling quarter are investigated for overlay or cash drag. Advisors should not use performance screenshots in client materials unless compliance has approved the language.

Escalation
Suitability concerns go to me and to Compliance. System problems go to #it-ops, and anything affecting client holdings should also be posted in #wealth-team so advisors are aware before client calls.

Questions about this guide can be sent to Grace Lin.

title: SanctionsScreen Tuning Report
text:
SanctionsScreen Tuning Report
Author: Anthony Ramirez, Compliance Analyst
Last updated: 2026-07-27
Audience: Compliance, Operations, Technology, Lending, Wealth Management

Purpose
This report summarizes the Q3 tuning review of SanctionsScreen, our OFAC and sanctions list screening service, with a focus on false positive volume and its downstream effect on KYCPipeline onboarding turnaround. It covers the review window of 2026-06-01 through 2026-07-24 and proposes threshold changes for sign-off by Marcus Bell. No client-level details are included; where an example is needed, it is described generically.

Summary of Findings
SanctionsScreen is performing within its recall requirements, but alert precision is poor for a subset of name types. Roughly 3.1% of onboarding screens generated a potential match alert during the window, and about 94% of those were closed as false positives after analyst review. The alert queue added an average of 1.4 business days to KYCPipeline cases that hit a screening alert, versus same-day clearance for cases that did not. Wealth Management and Lending onboarding are the most affected because both depend on KYCPipeline completing before accounts or loans proceed in ClientHub and LoanOrigination.

Main Drivers of False Positives
We sampled 400 closed alerts and categorized the cause of each.

1. Common transliterated names (Arabic, Cyrillic, and Chinese romanizations): about 38% of sampled alerts. The fuzzy match threshold of 85 catches spelling variants of listed individuals but also unrelated people with very common given names.
2. Entity name tokens: about 24%. Generic words such as Trading, Holdings, and Maritime match listed vessel operators and shell entities on partial token overlap.
3. Missing secondary identifiers: about 19%. Cases where date of birth or country was not populated in ClientHub, so the engine could not use secondary attributes to suppress the match. John Smith and Luis Bowen in KYC confirm this is mostly an intake form issue rather than a screening logic issue.
4. Stale list entries and delisted parties: about 6%. A delisted-party sync lag of up to 48 hours was observed once in June.
5. Other or uncategorized: about 13%.

Proposed Tuning Changes
Proposal A: Raise the individual-name fuzzy threshold from 85 to 88 only when at least two secondary identifiers are present and do not conflict with the listed record. Where fewer than two identifiers exist, the threshold stays at 85. Back-testing against the 400 sampled alerts plus 60 known true-positive test records showed a projected 31% reduction in alert volume with no loss of true-positive detection.

Proposal B: Add a token weighting rule for entity names so that generic terms (Holdings, Trading, Group, Capital, Maritime) contribute less to the match score. Back-testing projects a further 14% reduction in entity alerts. Vessel and aircraft matches remain at full weight.

Proposal C: Make country and date of birth required fields in the ClientHub onboarding form for individuals before the case can be submitted to KYCPipeline. This needs a change request with Grace Lin's team and Technology support from Leo Martinez.

Proposal D: Reduce list sync verification from a 24 hour polling interval to a 4 hour interval, with an alert to #compliance if a published list update has not been ingested within 6 hours.

Risk Assessment
The tuning changes were reviewed with Owen Gallagher's team for model risk considerations. The principal residual risk is that raising the threshold could suppress a legitimate match on a heavily altered name. To mitigate this, we propose keeping a 5% random sample of suppressed near-matches routed to a weekly QA review by Nadia Petrov, and retaining a hard override so that any name scoring 80 to 87 against a primary SDN entry is always reviewed regardless of identifiers. Daniel Sanchez will own the QA sample review for the first two months.

Operational Impact
If A and B are approved, expected analyst workload drops from about 62 alerts per day to about 34. That frees capacity during the KYCPipeline ownership transition to Compliance on 2026-10-06, when the team will absorb the onboarding queue currently handled by Operations. Ravi Patel's team has agreed to share its alert triage runbook before the transition.

Testing and Rollout Plan
Jenna Cho's engineering group will implement A, B, and D in the staging environment by 2026-08-14. We will run both rule sets in parallel (shadow mode) for three weeks, comparing alerts, and report the results in #compliance. Production cutover is targeted for the week of 2026-09-08, outside quarter-end reporting activity. Rollback is a configuration flag and can be completed in under 15 minutes.

Open Items
Sign-off on thresholds from Marcus Bell is pending. The ClientHub field change in Proposal C needs prioritization. We also need Technology to confirm DocVault retention of screening evidence for alerts closed under the new rules.

Next Steps
I will circulate the back-test workbook this week and schedule a review session with Compliance, Risk, and Wealth Management. Questions can go to me directly or to #compliance.

title: DataLake Architecture Overview
text:
DataLake Architecture Overview
Owner: Technology (Data Engineering)
Author: Michael Jones, Data Engineer
Last updated: 2026-07-28
Classification: Internal

Purpose
This document describes how the DataLake is structured, what feeds it, and which downstream systems rely on it. It is intended for engineers on call in Technology and for the Risk, Compliance, and Lending teams that own consumers of the lake. DataLake is classified as a standard-tier system, but several critical systems sit downstream of it, so treat incidents with that in mind.

Dependency Position
In the platform dependency graph DataLake has no upstream dependencies. It is a landing zone, and producers push into it. We deliberately avoid pull-based ingestion from other production services, so an outage in a source system never blocks the lake from starting or serving.

Downstream consumers are:
- FraudScore (Compliance): feature tables for real-time transaction scoring
- AMLMonitor (Compliance): transaction history and counterparty aggregates for alert generation
- CreditScoring (Lending): historical performance data for the decisioning models
- ReportingBI (Risk): management and regulatory dashboards

Because FraudScore and AMLMonitor are critical and depend on the lake, and PaymentsGateway depends on FraudScore, a prolonged DataLake stall can propagate to payments. The freshness monitors described below exist for that reason.

Layers
The lake is organized into three zones.

Raw zone: immutable, append-only copies of what producers send, partitioned by source and business date. Nothing in this zone is edited. If a producer sends bad data, we land a correction and let the curated layer reconcile it.

Curated zone: cleaned, conformed, and deduplicated tables with consistent keys for instruments, accounts, and legal entities. Schema changes here go through a review by Data Engineering plus the consuming team lead.

Serving zone: purpose-built marts for each consumer, for example the feature tables FraudScore reads and the reporting marts behind ReportingBI. Marts are rebuilt on a schedule and are safe to drop and regenerate from curated data.

Ingestion Sources
PricingSvc publishes end-of-day valuation snapshots and curve data to the raw zone as files. This is a push from PricingSvc, so the lake does not call it. Intraday ticks are not stored here; MarketDataFeed retains those, and only the closing set reaches us via PricingSvc.

Other feeds include general ledger extracts from GLCore, position snapshots from PositionStore, payment events from PaymentsGateway, and client reference data exports from ClientHub. Each feed has a named producer contact and an expected arrival window documented in the feed registry.

Access and Identity
Human access to query tooling and notebooks is authenticated through AuthSSO, with entitlements mapped to AD-style groups per team. Pipeline service accounts are managed separately inside the lake's own secrets store so that an AuthSSO disruption does not stop batch loads. Data Engineering reviews entitlements quarterly with Compliance.

Sensitive client attributes are tokenized at the curated layer. Analysts working in the serving zone see surrogate client keys, not names or contact details. Any request for re-identification goes through Compliance and is logged.

Scheduling and Freshness
Batch loads run overnight after the GLCore close. The target is for all curated tables to be refreshed by 05:30 Eastern, ahead of the morning Risk reporting run. Freshness monitors alert the Technology on-call in #it-ops when a table misses its window, and page if a table feeding FraudScore or AMLMonitor is more than two hours late.

Known Limitations
- Backfills of more than 90 days compete with nightly loads and should be scheduled on weekends.
- Lineage tracking is partial for older ReportingBI marts; we are migrating these to the standard build framework.
- ReconLegacy does not read from the lake and continues to use its own Oracle store.

Operational Runbook Pointers
For a late feed, first confirm with the producer team whether the file was sent, then check the raw zone landing log. For a failed curated build, rerun the single table before rerunning the whole DAG. For a consumer complaint about stale data, check the freshness dashboard before escalating.

Questions go to Michael Jones or the Data Engineering rotation in #it-ops.

title: OMS User Guide for Traders
text:
OMS User Guide for Traders
Owner: Daniel Reyes, Head of Trading
Last updated: 2026-07-29
Audience: Trading desk (equity traders, sales traders, execution traders, trading associates, quants with order entry rights)

Purpose
This guide covers day-to-day use of the OMS, the order management system for the trading desk, and how it connects to the TradeBlotter. It is a working reference, not a policy document. Where it conflicts with the Compliance or Risk manuals, those manuals win. No client names or account identifiers belong in free-text fields in the OMS; this guide therefore contains none, and you should not add any to order notes.

System Dependencies You Should Know
The OMS depends on PricingSvc for instrument prices and on AuthSSO for login and entitlements. The TradeBlotter depends on both the OMS and PricingSvc. In practice this means:
- If AuthSSO is degraded, you may be unable to log in or your entitlements may fail to load. Do not share sessions or credentials; raise it in #it-ops.
- If PricingSvc is stale, reference prices and limit checks in the OMS may be wrong, and blotter P&L will drift. Treat any price flagged stale as untradeable for limit-sensitive orders.
- Downstream, the SettlementEngine consumes executed trades from the OMS, so a booking error here becomes a settlement break later.

Logging In and Entitlements
Log in through AuthSSO with your firm credentials and MFA. Entitlements are role-based: execution traders can route and amend, sales traders can enter and allocate on behalf of coverage, trading associates have enter and cancel-own rights only, and quants have read access plus staged-order entry for approved strategies. Requests for changes go to your desk head, then to Technology via the access ticket queue. Entitlement changes are not instant; allow one business day.

Entering an Order
1. Open the order ticket and select the instrument from the security master. Confirm the identifier, not just the ticker.
2. Choose side, quantity, order type (market, limit, VWAP, TWAP, or participation), and time in force.
3. Select the book. Principal, agency, and wealth flow books are separate; picking the wrong one is the most common booking error we see.
4. Add a short, factual note if needed. Keep it to the order rationale or instruction reference.
5. Submit. Pre-trade checks run automatically against position and notional limits and restricted-list status.

Pre-Trade Checks and Overrides
Hard blocks cannot be overridden by traders. Soft warnings, such as notional above the single-order guideline or a price deviating more than the tolerance from the last reference price, require a written acknowledgement. If an instrument is on the restricted or watch list, stop and contact Compliance in #compliance before doing anything else. Repeated overrides are reviewed weekly by me and by Market Risk.

Amending and Cancelling
Amendments to quantity or limit price create a replace request with the venue. Until the venue confirms, the order shows as pending replace; do not resend. If you see a pending state lasting more than a minute, call the execution desk before cancelling, to avoid a double fill.

Allocations
Block orders are allocated after the fill using the allocation template on the ticket. Sales traders own allocations for their coverage. Allocations must be complete before the end-of-day cutoff so that the SettlementEngine picks up the correct splits. Late or partial allocations should be flagged to Operations the same day.

Using the TradeBlotter
The TradeBlotter is the live view of your orders, fills, positions, and intraday P&L. Key points:
- P&L is computed from OMS fills and PricingSvc marks. It is indicative, not the official book of record. Official P&L comes from the finance close.
- Use the filter bar to scope by book, desk, or strategy. Saved views are personal; the shared views maintained by the desk are read-only.
- If a fill appears in the OMS but not on the blotter within a few seconds, refresh once, then report it. Do not re-enter the trade.
- Exporting the blotter to a spreadsheet is permitted for desk analysis only. Do not send exports outside the firm.

End-of-Day Checklist
- All working orders are either cancelled or intentionally carried (GTC) with a note.
- Allocations complete and unmatched fills cleared.
- Blotter positions agree with your own tally for the books you run.
- Any breaks or manual adjustments are posted in #trading-desk or passed to Operations, who reconcile them in #recon.

When Things Go Wrong
For an OMS outage or order routing failure, call the desk head first, then post in #incidents with the time, the affected books, and the order references involved. Use the voice execution fallback only with approval from me or the senior execution trader on shift, and log every manually executed trade so it can be booked once the OMS is back. For slowness or access problems that are not outages, use #it-ops.

Training and Questions
New joiners complete an OMS walkthrough with an execution trader in their first week and are signed off before live order entry. Questions about this guide or suggestions for changes can go to me directly. Changes to checks and limits are made only through Risk and Compliance approval and are announced on #trading-desk.

title: Wire Transfer Operating Procedures
text:
Wire Transfer Operating Procedures
Owner: Ravi Patel, Head of Operations
Last updated: 2026-07-29
Applies to: Wire Room, Payments, and Settlements staff in Operations

Purpose
This procedure describes how Operations receives, validates, releases, and books outgoing and incoming wire transfers. It is the standard for everyone working in the WireRoom console and supports the controls expected by Compliance and Risk. If something here conflicts with a direct instruction from Compliance, follow Compliance and tell me afterwards.

No Personal Data in Tickets or Chat
No client names, account numbers, routing numbers, SWIFT/BIC codes, or IBANs may be typed into Slack, email, or free-text ticket fields. No placeholders are provided for these details in this document, so refer to the transaction by its internal wire reference and the word "client" only. Beneficiary details live in the payment record itself and are viewed only inside WireRoom.

Roles
Wire Room Specialists (Greg King, Derrick Anderson, Mike Herrera) key, verify, and release wires. Payments Specialists (Craig Garner, Ronald Lewis) own ACH batches, rejects, and returns. Settlements Specialists (Wayne Foster, Brian Hernandez) handle securities-related cash movements that originate from SettlementEngine. Compliance provides sanctions and AML review. I approve exceptions to this procedure.

Intake and Validation
1. Every wire request must arrive through the approved request form or a ticket. Verbal and email-only requests are not accepted.
2. The requester must be an authorized signer on file, or a Relationship Manager or Wealth Advisor acting on documented client instructions.
3. The initiating specialist confirms the instruction against the standing instruction record. Any change to beneficiary details triggers a callback to the client using the contact on file, never a number given in the request.
4. The specialist checks the request for completeness: amount, currency, value date, purpose, and funding source.

Sanctions and Fraud Checks
All wires pass through PaymentsGateway, which depends on FraudScore for real-time scoring. Sanctions screening runs against SanctionsScreen. A wire with a FraudScore hold or a sanctions hit may not be released by Operations. Route it to Compliance through #compliance or the AML queue, and wait for written clearance. Do not tell the requester the reason for a hold beyond "under review."

Dual Control and Limits
Every wire requires a maker and a checker, and they must be different people. Thresholds:
- Up to $250,000: one checker from the Wire Room.
- $250,001 to $2,000,000: checker plus Payments or Settlements lead sign-off.
- Above $2,000,000: checker plus my approval, or the approval of the COO, Linda Brandt, if I am unavailable.
Splitting a payment to stay below a threshold is prohibited and must be reported to Compliance.

Cut-off Times
Outgoing domestic wires must be released by 4:30 PM ET. International wires should be released by 12:00 PM ET to allow for correspondent processing. Requests that arrive after cut-off roll to the next business day unless I approve an exception. Do not promise same-day value after cut-off.

General Ledger Booking
When a wire is released, PaymentsGateway posts the cash entry to GLCore. The maker confirms the posting appears with the correct ledger account, currency, and value date. Securities-related cash movements arriving from SettlementEngine are booked against the settlement cash accounts, and Settlements staff verify them against the day's clearing report. If GLCore is unavailable, stop releasing wires and post in #incidents. Do not release manually and post later.

Daily Reconciliation
Tasha Greene and the Reconciliation team compare WireRoom activity, bank statements, and GLCore at end of day. Breaks are logged in #recon with the wire reference and age. Any break older than one business day is escalated to me. Unmatched incoming funds are held in suspense and never applied without client identification confirmed by the relevant Relationship Manager.

Rejects, Returns, and Recalls
If a wire is rejected or returned, the Payments Specialist documents the reason code, notifies the requester, and reverses the GLCore entry the same day. Recall requests need the same dual control as the original wire. Suspected fraud recalls go to Compliance immediately and are marked urgent.

Record Retention
Tickets, approvals, callback notes, and screening results are retained per the firm records policy. Attachments are stored in DocVault, not on shared drives or personal devices.

Exceptions and Questions
Raise exceptions with me in writing. For system issues with WireRoom or PaymentsGateway, open an incident and notify Technology through #it-ops. For regulatory questions, contact Marcus Bell's team in Compliance. Reviewed twice a year, and any change to thresholds must be approved by Risk and Compliance before it takes effect.

title: HELOC Product Guide
text:
HELOC Product Guide
Owner: Brian Kowalski, Head of Lending
Last updated: 2026-07-30
Audience: Lending, Wealth Management, Compliance, Risk, Operations

Purpose
This guide describes how Halcyon Ridge Capital originates, underwrites, closes, and services Home Equity Lines of Credit (HELOCs). It is the working reference for relationship managers, loan officers, underwriters, and the partner teams who touch a HELOC file. If something here conflicts with the Credit Policy Manual, the Credit Policy Manual wins; please tell me so we can fix this guide.

Product Overview
Our HELOC is a revolving line secured by a first or second lien on a borrower's primary or secondary residence. It is offered mainly to existing Wealth Management clients and to Lending referrals. Key terms:
- Draw period: 10 years, interest-only payments
- Repayment period: 20 years, fully amortizing
- Rate: variable, indexed to Prime plus a margin set by pricing tier
- Maximum combined loan-to-value (CLTV): 80% for primary residences, 70% for second homes
- Line size: $100,000 minimum, $2,500,000 maximum; anything above $1,000,000 needs Head of Lending sign-off
- Minimum credit score: 700 for standard tier, 740 for preferred pricing

Origination Workflow
1. Referral and intake. Relationship Managers in Lending (Brendan Alvarez, Lynn Chase) or Wealth Management (David Montes, Scott Hawkins) open the opportunity in ClientHub and attach the request summary. Loan Officers (Heidi Davis, Cassandra Hampton) own the file from that point.
2. Application. The Loan Officer creates the application in LoanOrigination, which pulls the client profile from ClientHub. Do not re-key client data; if ClientHub is wrong, fix it at the source.
3. KYC/CDD. LoanOrigination depends on KYCPipeline, so no file can advance past application until the client shows a cleared KYC status. Please note that ownership of KYCPipeline moved from Operations to Compliance effective 2026-10-06; questions about screening holds should go to the Compliance KYC specialists (John Smith, Luis Bowen) after that date, and to Operations before it. Sanctions hits are handled by Compliance through SanctionsScreen and are never cleared by Lending.
4. Credit decisioning. Credit Analysts (Jasmine Johnson, Brandi Palmer) run the CreditScoring model, which draws on DataLake, and prepare the credit memo. Senior Underwriters (Joshua Gordon, Tammy Murphy) make the decision within their authority.
5. Collateral. Order an appraisal or automated valuation, a title search, and confirm hazard insurance. Documents are stored in DocVault, which requires AuthSSO access; request access through #it-ops if you cannot open a file.
6. Closing. The Loan Closer (Brandon George) prepares closing documents, confirms the rescission period has expired for primary residences (three business days), and schedules recording of the lien.
7. Funding and setup. Operations releases any initial draw through PaymentsGateway after wire verification, and the accounting entries post to GLCore.

Underwriting Standards
- Maximum debt-to-income ratio of 43% including the proposed line at full utilization
- Documented income and asset verification for all lines above $500,000
- Interest-only draw payments are underwritten at a stressed rate of Prime plus 2.00% to test affordability
- Concentration limits: HELOC exposure in any single metro area is monitored by Credit Risk (Lance Peters, Phillip Jackson, John Garcia) and reviewed monthly
- Exceptions require written approval from the Senior Underwriter and a second sign-off from the Head of Lending; Risk is copied on all exceptions above 5% of monthly volume

Wealth Management Coordination
When a HELOC is being used to fund a securities purchase or a portfolio strategy, the Wealth Advisor must flag it to Lending before application. Portfolio Managers should record the intended use in PortfolioMgr notes. Lines pledged against or alongside a securities-backed facility must be reviewed jointly by Grace Lin's team and Lending to avoid duplicate collateral claims.

Compliance and Monitoring
- Every HELOC file must contain evidence of completed KYC, sanctions screening, and the required disclosures
- Draws are monitored by AMLMonitor; rapid full draws followed by outbound wires are routed to Compliance for review
- Wire requests from a HELOC draw go through WireRoom, which depends on PaymentsGateway and therefore FraudScore. A fraud hold is not overridden by Lending
- Suspicious activity is escalated to Nadia Petrov's AML group; do not discuss a potential SAR with the client

Servicing and Reporting
- Monthly interest statements are generated by the servicing batch and reconciled by Operations; breaks are posted in #recon
- ReportingBI publishes the HELOC portfolio dashboard (balances, utilization, delinquency) using RiskEngine, GLCore, and DataLake feeds. If numbers look stale, check #it-ops before escalating
- Delinquency over 30 days triggers a handoff to the Lending servicing queue and a notice to the relationship owner

Common Pitfalls
- Starting a file before KYC clears causes rework and aged pipeline
- Missing flood zone determinations delay closing
- Skipping the rescission calendar check leads to premature funding

Contacts
Product questions: Brian Kowalski. Underwriting: Joshua Gordon or Tammy Murphy. Closing: Brandon George. Compliance: Marcus Bell's team via #compliance. System issues: #it-ops, or #incidents for outages. Suggested edits to this guide are welcome at any time.

title: Model Risk Management Policy
text:
Document owner: John Garcia, Credit Risk Analyst, Risk
Last updated: 2026-08-04
Applies to: Trading, Wealth Management, Lending, M&A Advisory, Compliance, Risk, Operations, Technology

Purpose
This policy sets out how Halcyon Ridge Capital identifies, validates, approves, monitors and retires quantitative models. A model is any method that applies statistical, economic, financial or machine-learning techniques to turn inputs into estimates that inform a business or control decision. The goal is to ensure that model outputs are fit for purpose and that the limits of each model are understood by the people relying on it.

Scope
The policy covers models in production and models in development, including vendor models and spreadsheets that meet the definition above. Examples include the intraday VaR and exposure calculations in RiskEngine, instrument valuation logic in PricingSvc, the credit decisioning models in CreditScoring, the fraud models in FraudScore, the transaction monitoring scenarios in AMLMonitor, and the rebalancing logic in PortfolioMgr. Simple arithmetic tools, reports and dashboards in ReportingBI are out of scope unless they embed a model.

Roles and Responsibilities
Model Owner: the business lead accountable for a model. For example, the Head of Lending owns CreditScoring models and the Head of Risk owns RiskEngine methodology. Owners must keep documentation current and attest annually.
Model Developer: the quant analyst, data engineer or software engineer who builds and changes the model. Trading quants and Technology engineers act as developers for most pricing and risk models.
Model Validator: a member of the Risk team independent of the developer and owner. Credit Risk Analysts validate credit models; the Market Risk Manager coordinates validation of market and pricing models.
Model Risk Committee: chaired by the Head of Risk, with the Chief Financial Officer, Chief Operating Officer and Chief Compliance Officer as members. It approves tiering, accepts residual risk and signs off on exceptions.
Compliance: reviews models that support sanctions, KYC, fraud and AML controls for regulatory fit, in partnership with the Compliance Engineering Lead.

Model Inventory and Tiering
Risk maintains the model inventory. Every model must be registered before it is used in production. Each model is assigned a tier:
Tier 1: high impact on capital, P&L, credit decisions or regulatory obligations. Examples are RiskEngine VaR, PricingSvc valuation and the AML and fraud models. Full independent validation is required before use and annually thereafter.
Tier 2: moderate impact. Validation is proportionate and refreshed every two years or on material change.
Tier 3: low impact. Owner self-assessment with a Risk review of documentation.
Tiering considers materiality, complexity, data quality, reliance on upstream systems and the degree of human override.

Development Standards
Developers must document the purpose, theory, assumptions, data sources, known limitations, and intended use. Inputs must be traceable. Where a model depends on another system, such as pricing models consuming MarketDataFeed through PricingSvc or credit models reading from DataLake, the dependency and its data quality controls must be written down. Code must be version controlled, peer reviewed and reproducible in a non-production environment.

Validation
Independent validation covers conceptual soundness, data integrity, implementation testing, outcome analysis and sensitivity or stress testing. For Tier 1 models, validators must also perform benchmarking against an alternative approach where feasible and backtesting against realized outcomes. Findings are rated high, medium or low. High findings block production approval unless the Model Risk Committee grants a time-limited exception. Validators issue a written report within 30 business days of receiving a complete package.

Change Management
Material changes require revalidation before release. Material changes include new methodology, new data sources, recalibration beyond agreed tolerances, and changes in intended use. Technology releases touching model code follow the standard change process in #it-ops, and the validator confirms sign-off before deployment. Emergency fixes may be deployed with Head of Risk approval but must be validated within 15 business days.

Ongoing Monitoring
Owners monitor performance against defined thresholds, such as VaR backtesting exceptions, score drift in credit models, and alert-to-case conversion rates in AML scenarios. Breaches are escalated to Risk within two business days. Persistent breaches trigger a review and, if needed, a restriction or retirement of the model. Monitoring results are summarized quarterly for the Model Risk Committee.

Model Overrides and Use Restrictions
Users may override model outputs only with documented rationale and approval from the model owner. Override frequency is tracked and reviewed. Models must not be used outside their approved scope.

Vendor Models
Vendor models receive the same tiering. Where source code is unavailable, validation focuses on outcome analysis, vendor documentation, and controls over inputs. Vendor changes must be notified to Risk.

Issue Management and Retirement
Findings are tracked to closure with owners and due dates. Models that are no longer used must be retired, with the inventory updated and archived documentation retained according to the firm's records policy.

Policy Review
This policy is reviewed annually by Risk and approved by the Model Risk Committee. Questions should be sent to the Risk team or posted in #risk.

title: Best Execution Policy
text:
Halcyon Ridge Capital
Best Execution Policy
Owner: Daniel Reyes, Head of Trading
Last updated: 2026-08-06
Applies to: Trading, Wealth Management, and any desk routing client or firm orders through OMS

Purpose
This policy sets out how Halcyon Ridge Capital seeks the best possible result for client orders and for orders placed on behalf of the firm. It describes the factors we weigh, how we monitor execution quality, and who is accountable. It supports our obligations under FINRA Rule 5310 and applicable SEC requirements, and it is reviewed with Compliance and Risk at least annually.

Scope
The policy covers equity and listed derivative orders, fixed income orders worked by the Sales Trading group, and wealth management orders sent to the desk for execution. Orders are captured and routed through OMS. Prices and valuations used for pre-trade checks come from PricingSvc, which is fed by MarketDataFeed. Lending and M&A Advisory activity is outside the scope of this policy.

Execution Factors
When handling an order we consider the following, in roughly this order of priority unless the client gives specific instructions:
1. Price, including price improvement relative to the prevailing NBBO or the best available quote.
2. Total cost, including commissions, fees, spread, and expected market impact.
3. Speed and likelihood of execution and settlement.
4. Order size and nature, including liquidity of the instrument and the urgency of the request.
5. Any other factor relevant to the order, such as venue reliability or information leakage risk.
For retail-sized orders, total consideration (price plus costs) is the dominant factor. For large or illiquid orders, Execution Traders may give greater weight to market impact and likelihood of completion.

Venue Selection and Routing
The Execution Traders maintain an approved venue list covering exchanges, alternative trading systems, and wholesale liquidity providers. Venues are added or removed only with sign-off from the Head of Trading and notice to Compliance. Smart order routing logic in OMS must be configured to the approved list. Any manual override of routing must be recorded in the order notes with a short rationale. Payment for order flow and rebates may not determine routing where they would conflict with the best result for the client.

Client Instructions
Where a client gives specific instructions, such as a limit price, a venue, or a time window, we execute according to those instructions, and the policy is satisfied to the extent of that instruction. Traders should flag to the client, through the relationship owner in Wealth Management, if an instruction is likely to prevent a better result on other factors.

Aggregation and Allocation
Orders may be aggregated only when it is likely to benefit each participating client or account and when allocation rules are fixed before the order is released. Partial fills are allocated pro rata unless a documented exception applies. Proprietary orders may not be given priority over client orders. Portfolio Managers using PortfolioMgr for rebalancing must submit batch orders with allocation instructions attached.

Monitoring and Review
Execution quality is monitored on three levels:
1. Real-time: Traders use TradeBlotter to monitor fills, slippage versus arrival price, and outstanding orders. Unusual slippage is escalated to the Head of Trading the same day.
2. Daily: Trading Associates review exception reports covering rejected orders, late fills, and trade-throughs, and confirm that routing overrides carry rationale notes.
3. Quarterly: The Quant Analysts produce a transaction cost analysis comparing execution results against benchmarks such as VWAP, arrival price, and venue-level fill rates. Results are presented to the Best Execution Committee.

Best Execution Committee
The committee is chaired by the Head of Trading and includes representatives from Compliance, Risk, Wealth Management, and Operations. It meets quarterly, reviews the TCA package, evaluates the venue list, and records decisions in minutes retained by Compliance. Material findings are reported to the Chief Compliance Officer and the Chief Operating Officer.

System Dependencies and Outages
Best execution relies on timely market data and pricing. If MarketDataFeed or PricingSvc is degraded, traders must confirm quote integrity against a secondary source before releasing orders and must note the condition on the order. If OMS or AuthSSO is unavailable, orders may be handled by phone only with Head of Trading approval and must be entered into OMS retroactively once service is restored. Incidents affecting execution are raised in #incidents and logged for the next committee review.

Settlement Considerations
Traders should be aware that execution choices affect settlement. Trades flow from OMS to SettlementEngine, and Operations settlements staff should be notified in advance of any unusual venue, settlement cycle, or booking arrangement.

Recordkeeping
Order tickets, routing decisions, override rationales, TCA reports, and committee minutes are retained for at least six years in accordance with firm retention standards. Records must be available to Compliance and Risk on request.

Training and Attestation
All Trading staff and Wealth Management personnel who place orders must complete best execution training on joining and annually after that, and must attest to this policy each January.

Breaches and Escalation
Suspected breaches must be reported to the Head of Trading and the Chief Compliance Officer without delay. Compliance determines whether remediation, client notice, or regulatory reporting is required. Failure to follow this policy may result in disciplinary action.

Questions
Contact Daniel Reyes in Trading or Marcus Bell in Compliance.

title: Expense and Travel Policy
text:
Halcyon Ridge Capital
Expense and Travel Policy
Owner: Catherine Hale, Chief Executive Officer
Last updated: 2026-08-11

Purpose and Scope
This policy sets out how employees of Halcyon Ridge Capital incur, document, and claim business expenses and travel costs. It applies to every employee across Trading, Wealth Management, Lending, M&A Advisory, Compliance, Risk, Operations, Technology, and the Executive Office. The goal is to let people do their jobs well while keeping spending reasonable, transparent, and auditable.

General Principles
Spend firm money as you would your own, but do not lose revenue or credibility to save a few dollars. Every expense must have a clear business purpose, be supported by an itemized receipt, and be submitted within 30 days of being incurred. Expenses submitted after 60 days require approval from the Chief Financial Officer, Martin Osei. Personal expenses, fines, traffic or parking penalties, and spouse or family travel costs are never reimbursable.

Approvals
Your direct manager approves your expense reports. Department heads approve their own reports with Linda Brandt, Chief Operating Officer, as the second approver. Reports from the Executive Office are reviewed by Martin Osei. Any single item over $2,500, and any trip estimated over $7,500 in total, needs pre-approval from your department head before booking. Nobody may approve their own expenses or those of a person who manages them.

Air and Rail Travel
Book through the firm's designated travel portal at least 14 days ahead where possible. Economy class applies to flights under 5 hours. Premium economy or business class is allowed for flights over 5 hours, subject to department head approval. Executive Office members may travel business class on any flight over 3 hours. For New York to Boston and New York to Washington, Acela or equivalent rail in standard business class is preferred over flying.

Lodging
Book business hotels at or below the portal's city caps: $425 per night in New York, San Francisco, and London, and $325 per night elsewhere. Exceptions are permitted when a deal or conference makes the cap unrealistic; note the reason on the report. Incidentals such as minibar, in-room movies, and spa services are not reimbursable.

Meals and Entertainment
Business meals while traveling are reimbursed up to $85 per person per day. Client and prospect entertainment is capped at $200 per head per event and must record the firm attendees and the business purpose. Do not record external attendee identities beyond organization name in the expense system. Alcohol is reimbursable only when consumed in moderation at a business meal. Gifts to clients or counterparties must not exceed $100 per recipient per year and must be pre-cleared with Compliance under the gifts and entertainment register maintained by Marcus Bell's team.

Ground Transportation
Use standard car services, taxis, rideshare, or public transit. Rental cars require a business justification and the firm's corporate insurance election. Mileage for personal vehicles is reimbursed at the current IRS rate. Late-night car service is covered for employees working past 9:00 pm, including Operations staff supporting settlement and wire cutoffs, and Trading staff supporting market events.

M&A Advisory and Deal Travel
Travel for live mandates may be billed back to the client under the engagement letter. Mark such expenses with the engagement code in the expense system so they can be recharged. Project-related spend for wall-crossed teams must be kept confidential: use the project code name rather than the counterparty name in descriptions.

Conferences and Training
Conference attendance requires department head approval and a short business case. Registration, travel, and lodging fall under this policy. Required regulatory and certification training for Compliance, Risk, and Lending staff is fully covered when approved in advance.

Technology and Equipment
Hardware and software purchases are not handled through expenses. Request them through Technology so they can be provisioned, secured, and authenticated through AuthSSO. Home-office stipends and mobile plans are governed by the separate remote work policy.

Submitting Expenses
Submit reports through the expense module in HRIS. Attach itemized receipts for every expense over $25. Lost receipts require a signed missing receipt declaration. Reports are reimbursed to the employee's payroll account on the next bi-weekly cycle after approval.
