Corporate card balances are the employee's responsibility to reconcile monthly, and unreconciled charges older than 45 days may be payroll-deducted.

Compliance and Audit
Finance and Compliance sample expense reports quarterly. Suspected misuse, duplicate claims, or falsified receipts are treated as a conduct matter and may lead to disciplinary action, including termination and recovery of funds. Questions about gifts, entertainment, or anything that could appear to be an improper payment should go to Compliance in #compliance before the spend occurs.

Questions
General policy questions go to Martin Osei or Linda Brandt. Questions about the expense module go to the HRIS administrators in the Executive Office. This policy is reviewed annually.

title: KYC and CDD Standards
text:
KYC and CDD Standards
Owner: Compliance (author: Daniel Sanchez, AML Investigator)
Last updated: 2026-08-18
Approved by: Marcus Bell, Chief Compliance Officer

Purpose
This standard sets out the minimum Know Your Customer (KYC) and Customer Due Diligence (CDD) requirements for every client onboarded by Halcyon Ridge Capital, across Wealth Management, Lending, Trading and M&A Advisory. It applies to all front-office staff who open or sponsor a relationship and to the Compliance and Operations staff who screen and approve them.

Scope and Systems
All onboarding is run through KYCPipeline, our client onboarding KYC/CDD screening pipeline. KYCPipeline pulls client records from ClientHub, collects supporting documents from DocVault, and calls SanctionsScreen for OFAC and sanctions list screening. No account, loan facility or trading line may be activated until KYCPipeline shows an approved status. LoanOrigination also depends on KYCPipeline, so Lending cannot move a file to credit decisioning with an open KYC item.

Ownership Transition
KYCPipeline is currently operated by Operations under Ravi Patel. Ownership transfers to Compliance on 2026-10-06. Until that date, pipeline defects and configuration changes go to Operations. From 2026-10-06, they go to Compliance, with Jenna Cho as engineering lead. Policy decisions on screening rules have always been Compliance's, and that does not change.

Standard Due Diligence
For every client the relationship owner must collect and the KYC Specialist must verify:
- Legal identity and a government-issued identification document, or formation documents for entities
- Residential or registered business address
- Nature and purpose of the relationship and the expected activity
- Source of funds, and source of wealth for wealth and lending clients
- Beneficial owners at or above 25 percent ownership, and any person with control, for entity clients
- Politically exposed person status, checked at onboarding and at each periodic review

Documents are stored only in DocVault. Do not keep copies in email, shared drives or chat. Do not paste client identifiers into Slack channels, including #kyc-pipeline.

Enhanced Due Diligence
Enhanced due diligence (EDD) is required where any of the following applies:
- Politically exposed persons and their close associates
- Clients with a nexus to a high-risk jurisdiction as listed in the current Compliance country matrix
- Complex ownership structures, including trusts and offshore holding companies
- Digital asset activity, pending the final output of the #crypto-policy working group
- Adverse media or a screening hit that cannot be cleared at first review

EDD cases need additional source of wealth corroboration, senior management sign-off from the relevant business head, and approval by Compliance before activation. Nadia Petrov's AML team reviews all EDD files.

Sanctions Screening
SanctionsScreen runs automatically at onboarding and on every list update. Screening covers the client, beneficial owners, controllers and authorized signatories. Potential matches are never cleared by the relationship owner. A KYC Specialist reviews each alert, documents the rationale, and escalates unresolved matches to the AML team the same business day. A confirmed match is blocked immediately and reported to the CCO.

Risk Rating and Periodic Review
Each client is rated low, medium or high at onboarding. Review cycles are:
- High risk: every 12 months
- Medium risk: every 24 months
- Low risk: every 36 months

A trigger event, such as a change in ownership, unusual activity flagged by AMLMonitor, or a SAR filing, prompts an off-cycle review regardless of schedule.

Roles and Responsibilities
Relationship owners in Wealth, Lending and M&A are accountable for complete, accurate onboarding information. KYC Specialists, including John Smith and Luis Bowen, verify documents and work screening alerts. The AML team handles EDD and escalations. Compliance Engineering maintains the pipeline rules. Operations supports the platform until the transition date.

Service Levels
A complete standard-risk file should be decided within three business days of the last document being received. EDD files have no fixed turnaround, and business pressure is not a reason to shorten them. Incomplete files are returned to the relationship owner with a list of missing items.

Record Retention
KYC records are kept for at least five years after the relationship ends, or longer where required by regulation or a legal hold. Retention is managed through DocVault.

Exceptions and Questions
Exceptions to this standard need written approval from the CCO. Questions can be posted in #compliance or sent directly to Daniel Sanchez.

title: Postmortem: PricingSvc stale prices (2026-08-14)
text:
Postmortem: PricingSvc stale prices (2026-08-14)
Author: Leo Martinez, Senior Engineer, Technology
Incident: INC-2026-0814-01 (SEV1)
Status: Final draft for review. This is a blameless postmortem. The goal is to fix systems and processes, not to assign fault.

Summary
From 09:31 ET to roughly 16:55 ET on Friday 2026-08-14, PricingSvc kept serving the last good prices it had received instead of current ones. The root cause was an expired vendor TLS certificate on the MarketDataFeed connection to our primary pricing vendor.

PricingSvc did not fail outright. It served stale cached prices with no error and no staleness signal. That is why the problem ran for more than four hours before anyone declared an incident.

Timeline (all times ET, 2026-08-14 unless noted)
09:31  The vendor certificate expires and the TLS handshake from the MarketDataFeed handler starts failing. The handler retries with backoff and logs at WARN only. No alert fires.
09:31 onward  PricingSvc keeps serving its last cached marks. Its health checks stay green because the service itself is up.
~11:30  Traders informally notice that some intraday marks are not moving. This is treated as a quiet tape.
13:40  OMS pre-trade price checks start rejecting a growing share of orders, because limit prices fall outside the tolerance band around the stale reference price.
13:47  I declare a SEV1 in #incidents.
13:52  The incident record is opened.
13:55  Daniel Reyes confirms OMS rejections and that TradeBlotter P&L is frozen.
14:03  Owen Gallagher reports that RiskEngine VaR is stale and intraday limit monitoring is not possible.
14:20  Ravi Patel flags the risk to SettlementEngine and to the overnight ReconLegacy run if prices are not backfilled.
15:38  Omar Brown finds the handshake failures in the MarketDataFeed handler logs and confirms that the certificate expired at 09:31.
16:50  The vendor issues a renewed certificate and Barbara Beard deploys it to the feed handler.
16:55  Live ticks resume and PricingSvc marks begin updating.
17:15  Incident resolved. Backfill of 09:31 to 16:55 prices begins.
2026-08-15 morning  The backfill completes. SettlementEngine's cycle runs late, and ReconLegacy produces breaks that Operations clears manually.

Root Cause
The primary vendor rotated its certificate chain, and the client-side certificate we present had a fixed expiry. The certificate was installed by hand in 2025. It was not in any inventory or renewal calendar, so nobody owned its renewal.

Three contributing factors turned a short outage into a long silent one:
1. The feed handler treats handshake failures as retryable and does not escalate.
2. PricingSvc has no staleness threshold on cached prices.
3. Downstream systems cannot tell a stale price from a fresh one.

Impact
Direct consumers of PricingSvc:
RiskEngine: VaR and exposure figures were stale all afternoon, so Risk could not monitor limits.
OMS: orders were rejected on price checks from about 13:40 until recovery. The desk worked a small number of orders manually by phone with the executing brokers.
TradeBlotter: P&L was frozen.
PortfolioMgr: Wealth Management halted scheduled rebalancing.

Second-order effects:
SettlementEngine: delayed the next morning, because it depends on OMS trade data that was late and incomplete.
ReportingBI: dashboards fed by RiskEngine showed stale exposure until the backfill finished.
ReconLegacy: the end-of-day batch depends on SettlementEngine and GLCore, so it generated breaks. Tasha Greene and the recon team cleared them by mid-morning Saturday.

No client-facing pricing errors have been identified. No regulatory reporting deadline was missed.

What Went Well
Once the incident was declared, every affected team flagged its impact within 35 minutes. The vendor turned around the certificate renewal quickly. The backfill tooling worked on the first run.

What Went Poorly
It took more than four hours to detect the problem. Health checks measured whether the service was up, not whether its data was fresh. Ownership of the certificate was unclear.

Action Items
AI-1  Add price staleness alarms to PricingSvc. Page if more than 2% of active instruments have not ticked in 5 minutes during market hours. Owner: Leo Martinez. Due 2026-08-28.
AI-2  Put every vendor and client TLS certificate into central inventory with 30, 14, and 3-day expiry alerts. Owner: Omar Brown. Due 2026-09-04.
AI-3  Escalate repeated MarketDataFeed handshake failures to a page after 3 consecutive failures. Owner: Barbara Beard. Due 2026-08-28.
AI-4  Onboard a secondary market data vendor with automatic failover in MarketDataFeed. Owner: Sam Okafor, with Daniel Reyes for vendor selection. Target Q4 2026.
AI-5  Add graceful degradation in OMS. Flag stale reference prices on the order ticket and allow supervised override instead of hard rejection. Owner: Kevin Zhao with the Trading desk. Due 2026-09-30.
AI-6  Expose a price-age field in PricingSvc responses so RiskEngine and PortfolioMgr can mark outputs as stale. Owner: Angelica Schneider. Due 2026-09-18.
AI-7  Document PricingSvc consumers and failover behavior. Owner: Leo Martinez. Due 2026-09-02.

title: FraudScore Model Card
text:
FraudScore Model Card
Owner team: Compliance
Author: Luis Bowen, KYC Specialist
Last updated: 2026-08-20
System: FraudScore (critical tier)

Purpose
FraudScore provides real-time fraud scoring for transactions that move through the firm, with the ACH and wire flows handled by PaymentsGateway as the primary consumer. Each transaction receives a risk score between 0 and 1000 and a recommended action: release, hold for review, or reject. FraudScore also feeds AMLMonitor, which uses the scores as one input to its transaction monitoring and alert generation. This card summarizes what the model does, how it was built, where it is reliable, and where analysts should apply extra judgment. It is written from the KYC and onboarding perspective, so it emphasizes how scores interact with new client activity.

Intended Use
- Score outbound and inbound ACH and wire transactions before release by PaymentsGateway.
- Prioritize the WireRoom review queue so Wire Room Specialists see the highest risk items first.
- Supply a behavioral risk signal to AMLMonitor for downstream alerting.
- Support KYC refresh reviews by showing score trends for recently onboarded clients.

Not Intended For
- Final decisions on account closure or client exit. A score alone is never grounds for action.
- Sanctions determinations. Those belong to SanctionsScreen, which is independent of this model.
- Credit decisioning. CreditScoring in Lending is a separate model with separate governance.
- Trading surveillance or market abuse detection.

Model Overview
The production model is a gradient boosted tree ensemble with a small rules overlay. Features are computed from the DataLake, which FraudScore depends on, and refreshed on a rolling basis. Feature groups include transaction amount relative to client history, velocity over 1 hour, 24 hours, and 30 days, counterparty novelty, time of day and channel, payment instruction changes in the prior 14 days, and account age. The rules overlay forces a hold on a short list of patterns regardless of score, such as a beneficiary change followed by a large wire within 24 hours.

Training Data
Training used historical transaction outcomes from the last 24 months, labeled using confirmed fraud cases, returned items, and analyst dispositions from the review queue. Confirmed fraud is rare, under 0.1 percent of volume, so the training set was downsampled on legitimate transactions and reweighted. Analyst dispositions introduce some label noise because reviewers differ in how they close borderline cases. Jenna Cho's compliance engineering team maintains the labeling pipeline and reconciles disposition codes quarterly.

Performance
At the current threshold of 700 for a hold, the model catches roughly 82 percent of confirmed fraud in backtesting while holding about 0.6 percent of total volume. Precision in the hold band is around 11 percent, which is typical for this class of problem and reflects the review capacity we have in the Wire Room. Scores above 900 have precision near 45 percent and are routed for immediate review. Thresholds are reviewed each quarter with Compliance leadership and Operations.

Known Limitations
- New clients: accounts under 60 days old have thin history, so scores skew higher and the hold rate roughly doubles. KYC should flag newly onboarded clients so reviewers expect this.
- Seasonal volume: quarter end and tax periods shift amount distributions and raise false positives.
- Counterparty novelty: legitimate first-time payments to vendors or deal counterparties, including M&A closing flows, often score high. Advisory teams should notify the Wire Room ahead of large scheduled payments.
- Upstream dependency: if DataLake feature refresh lags, scores are computed on stale features. The service emits a degraded flag in that case and reviewers should treat low scores as less reliable.
- Drift: fraud tactics change quickly, and performance on novel typologies such as authorized push payment scams is weaker than on account takeover patterns.

Fairness and Bias Considerations
The model does not use client demographic attributes, names, or geography at a granular level. Country is used only as a coarse risk tier aligned with the firm's high risk jurisdiction list. We monitor hold rates by client segment and onboarding cohort monthly to detect disproportionate impact, and any material gap is escalated to Marcus Bell as Chief Compliance Officer.

Monitoring and Governance
- Weekly: hold rate, score distribution, and queue ageing reviewed by Compliance analysts.
- Monthly: population stability index on key features and segment hold rates.
- Quarterly: threshold review, backtest on newest labeled data, and sign-off from Compliance and Risk.
- Model changes require a documented change request, validation by Risk, and a staged rollout with shadow scoring before enforcement.

Operational Notes
FraudScore is critical, so an outage affects PaymentsGateway and AMLMonitor. If FraudScore is unavailable, PaymentsGateway falls back to the rules overlay only and routes all wires above the manual review limit to the Wire Room. Incidents are reported in #incidents, and tuning questions go to #compliance.

Contacts
Model questions: Luis Bowen or Jenna Cho. Escalations: Marcus Bell. Infrastructure issues: Technology SRE on call.

title: Board memo: Pause on onboarding digital-asset clients
text:
To: Board Risk Committee
From: Catherine Hale, Chief Executive Officer
Date: August 20, 2026
Re: Pause on onboarding new clients whose wealth derives from digital assets

Recommendation
I recommend that the committee approve a pause on onboarding new clients whose wealth derives from digital assets, effective Saturday, August 22, 2026. The pause applies to new relationships across Wealth Management and Lending. Existing clients, including those with digital-asset holdings or history, are unaffected and will continue to be serviced and monitored under current procedures.

Background
On July 28 the Office of Financial Supervision sent a supervisory letter to our Chief Compliance Officer highlighting its new interim guidance on onboarding clients with crypto-derived wealth. The letter makes clear that OFS expects firms to show AML controls that can evidence source of funds and source of wealth for these clients, not simply collect attestations. OFS has said final guidance will follow but has not given a date.

In response, Marcus Bell opened Compliance assessment COMP-112 on August 4. The assessment, with analysis from Nadia Petrov, found that AMLMonitor cannot trace on-chain flows. AMLMonitor draws on DataLake and FraudScore, neither of which ingests blockchain data, and we have no blockchain analytics vendor under contract. As a result we cannot independently verify where a prospect's digital-asset wealth came from before it reaches us as fiat. At the time of the assessment, nine active wealth prospects fell into this category.

Risk Considerations
Owen Gallagher and the Risk team have raised separate concerns about custody and counterparty exposure to crypto custodians and exchanges, including concentration with a small number of providers and limited recourse in a failure. Owen has also asked, rightly, what our exit plan would be if OFS tightens its guidance after we have taken clients on. Today we do not have a good answer.

Commercial Considerations
The #crypto-policy working group has had a full and useful debate. Grace Lin has made a strong case for continuing: Wealth Management sees 14 prospects in the broader pipeline representing roughly $40M of potential AUM, and competitors are onboarding these clients. She proposed an enhanced due diligence approach as a bridge. Martin Osei weighed that revenue against the regulatory exposure and suggested this committee make the call. I take the commercial point seriously, but enhanced due diligence without on-chain tracing still leaves us unable to evidence source of funds, which is precisely what OFS has flagged.

Conditions for Lifting the Pause
I propose the pause be lifted when both of the following are met:
(a) A blockchain analytics capability is integrated into AMLMonitor so that Compliance can trace on-chain flows as part of onboarding and ongoing monitoring.
(b) OFS publishes its final guidance on digital-asset client onboarding, so that our controls can be tested against the final standard rather than interim expectations.
Compliance will report back to this committee when both conditions are satisfied, with a recommendation on the enhanced due diligence framework to apply on resumption.

Next Steps
If approved, Grace will brief the wealth advisors, Brian Kowalski will brief Lending, and Compliance will ask relationship managers to hold any in-flight onboarding of affected prospects. Technology will scope the AMLMonitor integration with Compliance in parallel so we are ready to move once a vendor is selected.

Catherine

decision.summary: Pause onboarding of new digital-asset clients

title: AML Program Overview
text:
AML Program Overview
Owner: John Smith, KYC Specialist, Compliance
Last updated: 2026-08-21
Approved by: Marcus Bell, Chief Compliance Officer

Purpose and Scope
This document summarizes how Halcyon Ridge Capital prevents, detects, and reports money laundering and sanctions exposure. It applies to all business lines: Wealth Management, Lending, Trading, and M&A Advisory. It covers every employee who onboards clients, moves money, or supports those activities. It does not replace the detailed procedures held by Compliance; it is the starting point for new joiners and for business teams who need to know what is expected of them.

Roles and Responsibilities
Marcus Bell, as Chief Compliance Officer, is accountable for the program and reports on it to senior management. Nadia Petrov, Senior AML Analyst, leads alert review and typologies work. Daniel Sanchez, AML Investigator, handles escalated cases. The KYC Specialists, including John Smith and Luis Bowen, run onboarding reviews and periodic refreshes. Jenna Cho, Compliance Engineering Lead, maintains the monitoring rules and system integrations with Technology.

Front-office staff, relationship managers, and loan officers are the first line of defense. They must know their clients, report unusual behavior, and never tip off a client about an internal review or a filing.

Client Onboarding and KYC
No account, loan, or advisory relationship may be opened until customer due diligence is complete. The KYCPipeline screens each new client against identity, ownership, and adverse media checks. Relationship managers capture the relationship in ClientHub, and supporting documents are stored in DocVault. Ownership of KYCPipeline moves from Operations to Compliance on 2026-10-06, and until that date Operations remains the system owner for support requests.

Higher-risk clients require enhanced due diligence. Examples include politically exposed persons, entities with complex or opaque ownership, clients in elevated-risk jurisdictions, and cash-intensive businesses. Enhanced reviews need source-of-wealth documentation and sign-off from a KYC Specialist and the Senior AML Analyst before activation.

Sanctions Screening
SanctionsScreen performs OFAC and other sanctions list screening. Clients, beneficial owners, and counterparties are screened at onboarding, whenever lists are updated, and when client details change. Payments are also checked before release. Potential matches must be held and sent to Compliance. Staff may not clear a possible match on their own, and the wire room must not release a held payment without written Compliance approval.

Transaction Monitoring
AMLMonitor generates alerts on transaction patterns such as structuring, rapid movement of funds, unusual wire activity, and activity inconsistent with the client profile. It draws on data from DataLake and works alongside FraudScore, which scores transactions in real time. Alerts are triaged by the AML analysts, who document the rationale for closing or escalating each one. Alert thresholds are reviewed at least twice a year, and changes are tested before release.

Suspicious Activity Reporting
When an investigation concludes that activity is suspicious, the case is moved into SARFiling. The investigator drafts the narrative, attaches evidence from DocVault, and submits it for review by the Chief Compliance Officer. Reports must be filed within the regulatory deadline, which runs from the date we determine the activity warrants a filing. SAR existence and contents are strictly confidential. Do not discuss them in public channels, with the client, or with colleagues who have no need to know.

Escalation: What to Do If You See Something
If you notice unusual activity, contact Compliance the same day through the #compliance channel for general questions, or by direct message to the AML team for anything sensitive. Do not put client-specific details in public channels. Reasonable suspicion is enough; you do not need proof.

Training and Record Retention
All employees complete AML training at hire and annually. Role-specific sessions are provided to Wealth Management, Lending, Operations, and the wire room. KYC files, screening results, alert dispositions, and SAR records are retained for at least five years after the relationship ends, or longer where regulators or legal holds require.

Independent Testing and Review
The program is tested independently each year, and findings are tracked to closure by Compliance with a status update to the CEO and the Board risk committee. This overview is reviewed every year and after any significant regulatory change or system ownership change.

title: Counterparty Credit Risk Methodology
text:
Counterparty Credit Risk Methodology
Owner: John Garcia, Credit Risk Analyst, Risk
Last updated: 2026-08-28
Reviewed by: Owen Gallagher, Head of Risk

Purpose
This document describes how Halcyon Ridge Capital measures, limits, and monitors counterparty credit risk arising from trading, settlement, lending, and wealth activity. It is intended for Risk, Trading, Lending, Operations, and Compliance staff who set up counterparties, request limit changes, or respond to limit breaches. It does not cover market risk limits, which are described in the Market Risk Manager's VaR methodology note.

Scope
The methodology applies to the following exposure types:
1. Settlement exposure on cash and securities trades booked through OMS and cleared through SettlementEngine.
2. Replacement cost exposure on derivatives and securities financing with institutional counterparties.
3. Pre-settlement exposure on open orders and unsettled positions.
4. Credit exposure on commercial and secured loans originated through LoanOrigination, where the borrower is also a trading or custody counterparty.

Counterparty Onboarding and Internal Rating
Before a counterparty can be enabled for trading in OMS, Credit Risk assigns an internal rating on a 1 to 10 scale (1 strongest). Inputs are audited financials, external agency ratings where available, leverage and liquidity ratios, jurisdiction, and sector. Credit analysts in Lending may contribute model outputs from CreditScoring, but the Risk rating is the one that governs limits. Ratings are proposed by a Credit Risk Analyst and approved by the Head of Risk. Ratings of 8 or worse require sign-off from the CFO, Martin Osei.

KYC and sanctions clearance must be complete before a rating is approved. Compliance confirms this through KYCPipeline and SanctionsScreen. A counterparty without a clean KYC status is blocked in OMS regardless of its rating.

Exposure Measurement
Exposure is calculated in RiskEngine using positions from PositionStore and valuations from PricingSvc, which in turn depends on MarketDataFeed. The following measures are used:
- Current exposure: the mark-to-market of positions with a counterparty, floored at zero per netting set, net of eligible collateral.
- Potential future exposure (PFE): the 95th percentile of simulated exposure over the remaining life of the trade set, using a Monte Carlo engine with 5,000 paths and a 10-day margin period of risk for margined sets.
- Settlement exposure: gross notional of trades due to settle in the next two business days, taken from SettlementEngine.
- Wrong-way risk add-on: applied where counterparty default probability is positively correlated with the underlying, for example a bank counterparty on its own bonds.

Netting and Collateral
Exposure is netted only where legal review has confirmed enforceability of the master agreement in the relevant jurisdiction. The netting flag is stored against the counterparty record and reviewed annually. Collateral is haircut by asset type: cash 0%, US Treasuries 2%, investment grade corporates 10%, listed equities 20%. Collateral without a current valuation from PricingSvc is excluded until the price is refreshed.

Limit Framework
Limits are set per counterparty on three dimensions: PFE, settlement exposure, and tenor. Starting limits by internal rating:
- Ratings 1 to 3: PFE up to $75M
- Ratings 4 to 5: PFE up to $40M
- Ratings 6 to 7: PFE up to $15M
- Ratings 8 and worse: PFE up to $3M, collateralized only

A firm-wide concentration limit caps aggregate exposure to any single group at 10% of regulatory capital and to any single sector at 25%. Limit increases above the starting band require approval from the Head of Risk and, above $50M, the CFO.

Monitoring and Escalation
RiskEngine refreshes exposure intraday. ReportingBI publishes the daily limit utilization dashboard by 7:30 AM ET, which depends on RiskEngine, GLCore, and DataLake being current. If any of those feeds is stale, the dashboard shows a data-quality banner and Credit Risk must not rely on it.

Utilization triggers:
- 80%: automated alert to the Credit Risk Analyst on duty and the desk head.
- 95%: Trading must obtain approval from Credit Risk before adding exposure.
- 100%: OMS blocks new risk-increasing orders for the counterparty. Risk-reducing orders are still allowed. Credit Risk posts in #risk and notifies the Head of Trading, Daniel Reyes.

Temporary excesses may be approved for up to five business days by the Head of Risk. Anything longer requires a formal limit review.

Stress Testing and Review
Credit Risk runs a monthly stress on the top 20 counterparties covering a two-notch downgrade, a 30% fall in collateral values, and a 20% widening in credit spreads. Results go to the Head of Risk and the COO, Linda Brandt. Every rating is reviewed at least annually, and quarterly for ratings of 6 or worse or on any watchlist name. Triggers for an immediate off-cycle review include an agency downgrade, a missed margin call, a failed settlement, delayed financial reporting, or adverse press.

Default and Watchlist Procedure
When a counterparty is placed on the watchlist, Credit Risk lowers limits, tightens collateral terms, and informs Trading, Operations, and Lending. On a default event, Operations halts settlement instructions, Legal is engaged, and Credit Risk calculates close-out exposure using the last good PricingSvc marks.

Model Governance
The PFE model is validated annually by an independent party. Changes to haircuts, correlation assumptions, or simulation parameters follow the change process and require Head of Risk approval. Known limitation: ReconLegacy break data is not yet fed into exposure calculations, so settlement fails are tracked manually by Operations and reported to Credit Risk each morning.

Contact
Questions should go to John Garcia or the #risk channel.

title: Market Risk Limits Framework
text:
Document owner: Christopher Jones, Risk Analyst, Risk
Approved by: Owen Gallagher, Head of Risk
Last updated: 2026-09-02
Applies to: Trading, Wealth Management (discretionary portfolios), and Treasury-related activity booked by Operations

Purpose
This policy sets out how Halcyon Ridge Capital defines, monitors, escalates, and reviews market risk limits. Its goal is to keep trading and portfolio activity within the risk appetite agreed by the CEO and CFO, and to give desk heads and the Risk team a common, auditable process. No client-specific or personal data is held in this document; limit utilization is reported at desk and book level only.

Scope and Ownership
The Risk team owns the limit framework. Paul Hansen, Market Risk Manager, administers day-to-day limit monitoring. Desk heads, including Daniel Reyes for Trading and Grace Lin for Wealth Management, are accountable for keeping their books inside limits. Owen Gallagher approves limit changes above delegated thresholds and reports material breaches to Martin Osei and Catherine Hale.

Limit Types
The framework uses four layers of limits:

1. Value at Risk (VaR): One-day 99% VaR limits set at firm, desk, and book level. VaR is calculated intraday by RiskEngine using prices from PricingSvc and holdings from PositionStore.
2. Notional and exposure limits: Gross and net exposure caps by asset class, sector, and issuer concentration.
3. Sensitivity limits: Delta, vega, and DV01 limits for desks carrying rates, options, or credit-spread exposure.
4. Stop-loss and drawdown triggers: Month-to-date and peak-to-trough loss thresholds that force a review of strategy and sizing.

Limit Setting and Calibration
Limits are set annually and reviewed quarterly. Proposals originate from the desk head, are stress-tested by Risk, and are approved according to the table of authority below. Calibration draws on historical and hypothetical stress scenarios, liquidity of the underlying instruments, and the capital allocated to the desk. Quantitative inputs are sourced from DataLake extracts reviewed by Risk before use.

Threshold Levels and Escalation
Every limit has three states:

Green: utilization below 80% of the limit. No action required.
Amber: utilization between 80% and 100%. The desk head is notified automatically and must confirm a plan to Risk within one business day.
Red: utilization above 100%. This is a breach. Trading in the affected book is restricted to risk-reducing orders until the breach is cured or a temporary excess is approved.

Breaches are escalated as follows: Market Risk Manager notifies the desk head immediately; the Head of Risk is informed within 30 minutes; the CFO and COO are informed the same day for any firm-level or repeated desk-level breach. Breaches lasting longer than two business days are reported to the CEO and logged for the next risk committee.

Temporary Excesses
A temporary excess may be granted only in writing by the Head of Risk, with a stated size, a stated expiry of no more than five business days, and a documented rationale. Excesses are recorded in the limit register and appear in ReportingBI with a distinct flag. Verbal approvals are not valid.

Monitoring and Reporting
RiskEngine produces utilization snapshots intraday and an end-of-day official figure. Risk analysts reconcile the official figure against PositionStore and GLCore-based P&L before it is published. ReportingBI carries the daily limit utilization dashboard for desk heads and the weekly summary for executives. If RiskEngine or its upstream feeds (PricingSvc, MarketDataFeed) are degraded, Risk applies the fallback procedure: the last validated snapshot is used, desks are told to freeze discretionary risk increases, and the incident is raised in #incidents.

Model Limitations and Overrides
VaR is a statistical estimate and does not capture tail events. Risk therefore maintains supplementary stress limits. Analysts may propose model overrides, such as a manual price for an illiquid instrument, but each override must be documented, reviewed by a second Risk analyst, and expire within ten business days.

Table of Authority
Desk-level limit increase up to 10%: Market Risk Manager
Desk-level limit increase above 10%: Head of Risk
Firm-level limit changes: Head of Risk with CFO approval
Permanent changes to the framework: Head of Risk, CFO, and COO

Review and Record Keeping
The limit register, breach log, and approval evidence are retained by Risk for at least seven years. This framework is reviewed every twelve months or sooner after any significant breach or regulatory change. Questions should be raised in #risk or sent to Christopher Jones.

title: PricingSvc architecture and consumers
text:
PricingSvc architecture and consumers
Author: Leo Martinez, Senior Engineer, Technology
Last updated: 2026-09-02
This document closes action item AI-7 from the 2026-08-14 stale prices postmortem.

Purpose
PricingSvc is the firm's single source of instrument prices and valuations for intraday use. It is a critical-tier service owned by Technology. This document covers its upstream dependency, its consumers, its SLAs, its caching behavior, and what happens when it degrades.

Upstream
PricingSvc has one upstream dependency: MarketDataFeed. MarketDataFeed ingests real-time exchange and vendor data and normalizes it into a common tick format.

PricingSvc subscribes to that tick stream. It then:
derives marks (last, mid, and evaluated prices for less liquid instruments);
applies the end-of-day close policy;
publishes prices over a streaming API and a request/response API.

Today MarketDataFeed connects to one primary vendor. A secondary vendor is in procurement under AI-4, with Sam Okafor and Daniel Reyes leading selection.

Direct Consumers
RiskEngine (Risk): pulls marks to compute intraday VaR and exposure. RiskEngine also depends on PositionStore for holdings.
OMS (Trading): runs pre-trade price-band checks against the PricingSvc reference price. OMS also depends on AuthSSO.
TradeBlotter (Trading): shows trader P&L. It reads prices directly from PricingSvc and order and fill data from OMS.
PortfolioMgr (Wealth Management): runs valuation and rebalancing using PricingSvc marks together with PositionStore holdings.

Indirect Consumers
These systems never call PricingSvc, but they inherit its failures:
SettlementEngine depends on OMS, and through it on trade flow.
ReportingBI depends on RiskEngine, along with GLCore and DataLake.
ReconLegacy depends on SettlementEngine and GLCore. On 2026-08-14 the breaks reached ReconLegacy through this path, not through any pricing call.

When planning maintenance or reviewing an incident, treat all of these systems as being in scope.

SLAs
Availability: 99.95% during market hours, 07:00 to 18:00 ET, Monday to Friday.
Latency: p99 under 50 ms for request/response calls. Streaming updates must arrive within 250 ms of the MarketDataFeed tick.
Freshness (new since the incident): during market hours, no more than 2% of active listed instruments may be more than 5 minutes old. A breach pages the on-call engineer. The alarm went live on 2026-08-27.
End-of-day closing marks: published by 17:30 ET for downstream batch jobs.

Caching
PricingSvc keeps a sharded in-memory cache of last-known prices for each instrument, with a warm replica in the secondary data center.

Before the incident, cached prices never expired and responses did not carry their age. Since AI-6 shipped, every response includes price_age_ms and a stale flag. The flag is set when an instrument's price age exceeds its asset-class threshold: 5 minutes for listed equities, longer for evaluated fixed income.

Consumers are expected to act on the flag:
RiskEngine labels VaR output as stale-input.
PortfolioMgr blocks automated rebalancing.
OMS behavior is described under Failover and Degradation.

Failover and Degradation
Service failover: PricingSvc runs active-active across two data centers behind the internal load balancer. Losing one node or one site is transparent to consumers.

Data failover: this is the weak point today. If the vendor feed stops, both sites serve the same stale cache. Until the secondary vendor is live, the mitigations are:
the freshness alarm;
MarketDataFeed paging after 3 consecutive handshake failures;
expiry alerts for every vendor certificate, now tracked in the certificate inventory Omar Brown maintains.

OMS degradation: Kevin Zhao is building graceful degradation, due 2026-09-30. When a reference price is flagged stale, OMS will show a warning on the order ticket and let a desk supervisor override the price check, instead of hard-rejecting the order.

Contacts
PricingSvc on-call: Technology SRE rotation.
Service owner: Leo Martinez.
Escalation: Sam Okafor.

For anything that touches a direct consumer, notify #it-ops and the owning team's channel before making changes.

title: Commercial Lending Credit Policy
text:
Commercial Lending Credit Policy
Owner: Brian Kowalski, Head of Lending
Last updated: 2026-09-04
Applies to: Lending, Risk, Compliance, Operations, and Wealth Management referral partners

Purpose
This policy sets the standards under which Halcyon Ridge Capital originates, underwrites, approves, closes, and monitors commercial loans. It is intended to keep credit quality consistent, ensure that every approval is traceable to a documented analysis, and align Lending with Risk and Compliance requirements.

Scope
The policy covers term loans, revolving credit facilities, and secured bridge facilities made to operating businesses and investment entities. Loans to individuals are covered by separate guidance. Any exception to this policy must be documented under the Exceptions section below.

Roles and Responsibilities
Relationship Managers in Lending source opportunities, collect initial financial information, and remain the primary contact through closing. Credit Analysts spread financials, build cash flow projections, and draft the credit memo. Senior Underwriters review each memo, challenge assumptions, and recommend a risk rating. Loan Officers manage documentation and conditions precedent. The Loan Closer confirms all conditions are satisfied before funding is released. Credit Risk Analysts in Risk provide an independent review for facilities above the thresholds listed below. The Head of Lending is accountable for portfolio performance and for adherence to this policy.

Systems of Record
All applications must be created and tracked in LoanOrigination. Client records live in ClientHub, and supporting documents must be stored in DocVault rather than shared by email or personal drives. Credit decisioning models run in CreditScoring, which draws on data from DataLake. Onboarding checks are completed through KYCPipeline before any facility can advance to approval. Note that KYCPipeline ownership moves from Operations to Compliance on 2026-10-06; Lending users should direct questions about screening status to the Compliance team from that date. Because LoanOrigination depends on ClientHub, CreditScoring, and KYCPipeline, an outage of any of these will pause new submissions, and Lending should follow the incident process in #incidents.

Underwriting Standards
Every credit memo must include: a summary of the borrower's business and purpose of the facility; three years of historical financials where available, plus the most recent interim period; a debt service coverage analysis; a leverage analysis; a description of the primary and secondary sources of repayment; collateral valuation and lien position; and an assessment of industry and concentration risk.
Guideline minimums for operating companies are a debt service coverage ratio of 1.25x on a historical and projected basis and total senior leverage not exceeding 3.5x EBITDA. Secured facilities should carry an advance rate that does not exceed 75 percent of appraised or independently verified collateral value. Facilities that fall outside these guidelines are treated as exceptions.

KYC and Sanctions Requirements
No facility may be approved until KYCPipeline shows a completed CDD review and a clear result from SanctionsScreen. Any adverse media, beneficial ownership gaps, or screening hits must be escalated to Compliance and resolved before the credit memo moves to committee. Lending staff must not override a Compliance hold.

Approval Authority
Senior Underwriters may approve new exposure up to $2 million per borrower relationship. Exposure from $2 million to $10 million requires approval by the Head of Lending plus a concurring review from Credit Risk. Exposure above $10 million, or any facility that would result in a single-name concentration above 5 percent of the commercial loan book, must go to the Credit Committee, which includes the Chief Financial Officer and the Head of Risk. Approvals must be recorded in LoanOrigination with the approver's name and date.

Pricing and Terms
Pricing should reflect the internal risk rating, tenor, collateral, and funding cost provided by Finance. Covenants must be set at levels that give early warning while leaving reasonable headroom. Standard covenants include minimum coverage, maximum leverage, and quarterly financial reporting within 45 days of period end.

Closing and Funding
The Loan Closer verifies executed documents, perfected liens, insurance evidence, and satisfaction of all conditions. Funding instructions are sent to Operations, where the Wire Room and Payments teams process disbursement through PaymentsGateway. Wire instructions must be verified by call-back using contact details already on file, never those supplied in the funding request.

Monitoring and Watchlist
Credit Analysts refresh ratings at least annually and after any covenant breach, missed payment, or material adverse event. Credit Risk reviews the watchlist monthly. Facilities risk rated at or below the internal watch grade must have a documented action plan, reviewed by the Head of Lending each month. Portfolio exposure reporting is available through ReportingBI.

Exceptions
Exceptions require a written rationale, identified mitigants, and approval one level above the normal authority. All exceptions are logged and reported to the Credit Committee quarterly.

Records and Review
Credit files must be retained in DocVault according to the firm's records schedule. This policy is reviewed annually, or sooner if regulation or portfolio conditions change. Questions can be sent to the Head of Lending or posted in #lending.

title: Month-End Close Procedures
text:
Document owner: Ravi Patel, Head of Operations
Last updated: 2026-09-07
Applies to: Operations, Finance, Technology, Risk, Compliance

Purpose
This procedure describes how Halcyon Ridge Capital closes the books each month. It covers the sequence of tasks, system dependencies, owners, and escalation paths. The goal is a signed-off general ledger in GLCore by close of business on business day 5 (BD+5), with all reconciliation breaks either cleared or documented.

Scope and Systems
The close centers on GLCore, our general ledger. GLCore has no upstream dependencies, but SettlementEngine and ReconLegacy both read from it, and ReportingBI uses it for management and regulatory dashboards. ReconLegacy is the legacy end-of-day reconciliation batch (Perl on Oracle 11g). It depends on SettlementEngine and GLCore, so it must not be run until both have completed their daily processing. Until a replacement is approved, ReconLegacy remains the system of record for the final month-end reconciliation run.

No personal or account-level client information belongs in close tickets, Slack posts, or emails. Reference breaks by internal ticket key, trade reference, or ledger entry id only.

Timeline Overview
BD-1: Pre-close checks
BD+1: Subledger cutoff and settlement sweep
BD+2: Reconciliation run and break triage
BD+3: Accruals, adjusting entries, and review
BD+4: Finance and Risk sign-off
BD+5: Final lock of the period in GLCore

BD-1: Pre-Close Checks
The Head of Operations confirms staffing and posts the close calendar in #recon. Settlements Specialists confirm there are no open settlement fails older than T+2. Payments Specialists confirm that all ACH and wire batches from PaymentsGateway have posted to GLCore. The Wire Room confirms there are no pending wires in WireRoom that would land after cutoff. Technology confirms no change freezes or maintenance windows overlap with the close and that Oracle 11g backups for ReconLegacy completed successfully.

BD+1: Cutoff and Settlement Sweep
At 18:00 ET on the last business day of the month, SettlementEngine posts its final batch to GLCore. Settlements Specialists verify the batch count and total against the OMS trade count. Any trade booked in OMS but not settled is listed in the cutoff exceptions sheet with an owner and an expected settlement date. Do not manually post entries to GLCore after cutoff without approval from the Head of Operations.

BD+2: Reconciliation Run and Break Triage
Once SettlementEngine and GLCore both show a completed status, the Reconciliation Analyst starts the ReconLegacy batch. The run normally takes about 90 minutes. If it fails or stalls, do not rerun it blindly. Post the error in #recon, open an incident if the run exceeds three hours, and page the on-call Technology engineer for the Oracle environment.

Breaks are triaged in three buckets:
1. Timing breaks, which clear within two business days and are carried with a note.
2. Amount breaks, which need an owner and a root cause in the ticket.
3. Unmatched items older than 30 days, which require escalation to the Head of Operations and the CFO's office.

Every break above $25,000 needs a named owner by end of BD+2. Aggregate breaks above $250,000 are reported to Risk the same day.

BD+3: Accruals and Adjusting Entries
Finance prepares accruals for fees, interest, and vendor invoices. Operations prepares adjusting entries for confirmed breaks. Every manual journal entry requires a preparer and a separate reviewer; no one approves their own entry. Attach supporting evidence to the GLCore entry, not to email.

BD+4: Review and Sign-Off
The Reconciliation Analyst produces the final break report. The Head of Operations reviews it and signs off for Operations. Finance, under the CFO, reviews the trial balance and variance commentary. Risk reviews the break report and confirms ReportingBI figures tie to GLCore before regulatory dashboards are refreshed.

BD+5: Period Lock
After all sign-offs are logged, Finance locks the period in GLCore. Late adjustments after lock go through a reopen request approved by the CFO and the Head of Operations, and they are documented in the close file.

Escalation
First contact for close issues is #recon. Technology issues go to #it-ops, and production-impacting problems go to #incidents. Unresolved items at BD+4 are escalated to the Chief Operating Officer.

Records Retention
The close file, including the cutoff exceptions sheet, final break report, journal entry approvals, and sign-off confirmations, is saved to the shared close folder and retained according to firm record-keeping policy.

Change History
2026-09-07: Clarified ReconLegacy rerun guidance and the break escalation thresholds. Updated by Ravi Patel.

title: Vendor Management Policy
text:
Vendor Management Policy
Owner: Catherine Hale, Chief Executive Officer
Last updated: 2026-09-08

Purpose
This policy sets out how Halcyon Ridge Capital selects, onboards, monitors, and exits third-party vendors. Our trading, wealth, lending, and advisory businesses rely on external data, infrastructure, and service providers. A failure at a vendor can become a failure at the firm, so every vendor relationship needs a named internal owner and a documented risk assessment.

Scope
This policy applies to every external organization that provides goods or services to the firm, or that touches firm systems or data. Examples include market data and pricing vendors feeding MarketDataFeed and PricingSvc, sanctions list providers supporting SanctionsScreen, payment network and bank connectivity providers behind PaymentsGateway, cloud and hosting providers, identity providers connected to AuthSSO, and outside consultants and contractors. It applies to all employees in all teams.

Roles and Responsibilities
Business Owner: The head of the team that sponsors the vendor. The Business Owner is accountable for the relationship, the business case, and the annual review.
Technology: Sam Okafor, Director of Engineering, or a delegate reviews technical integration, access scope, and architecture fit for any vendor connecting to a firm system.
Risk: Owen Gallagher, Head of Risk, assigns the vendor tier and signs off on concentration and operational resilience risk.
Compliance: Marcus Bell, Chief Compliance Officer, reviews regulatory, sanctions, AML, and data protection exposure.
Operations: Ravi Patel, Head of Operations, owns payment, settlement, and reconciliation-related vendors and verifies service levels against operational procedures.
Finance: Martin Osei, Chief Financial Officer, approves spend and reviews contract terms with material financial commitments.
COO: Linda Brandt maintains the central vendor register and chairs the quarterly Vendor Oversight Review.

Vendor Tiering
Every vendor is assigned one of three tiers before contract signature.
Tier 1 (Critical): The vendor supports a critical system, or an outage would halt trading, settlement, payments, or regulatory screening. Examples are providers for MarketDataFeed, SanctionsScreen, PaymentsGateway, and AuthSSO.
Tier 2 (Important): The vendor supports a standard system or handles confidential firm information, for example providers connected to DocVault, DataLake, or ClientHub.
Tier 3 (Low): No system access, no confidential data, and easy substitution.
The tier drives the depth of due diligence and the monitoring frequency described below.

Due Diligence
Before engagement, the Business Owner submits a vendor request through the procurement workflow. Required reviews:
1. Financial health review, including audited statements for Tier 1 and Tier 2 vendors.
2. Information security assessment, including independent audit reports where available and evidence of access controls, encryption, and incident response.
3. Compliance screening covering sanctions, adverse media, and ownership.
4. Business continuity and disaster recovery review, including tested recovery objectives for Tier 1 vendors.
5. Dependency mapping by Technology showing which firm systems and downstream systems rely on the vendor. For example, a pricing vendor failure affects PricingSvc, and therefore RiskEngine, OMS, TradeBlotter, and PortfolioMgr.
Tier 1 vendors also require Risk to document a fallback or substitute plan.

Contract Requirements
All Tier 1 and Tier 2 contracts must include: defined service levels with remedies, right to audit, breach notification within 24 hours of discovery, data return and deletion on termination, subcontractor disclosure, confidentiality terms, and regulatory cooperation clauses. Legal review is mandatory. No employee may sign a vendor contract outside delegated signing authority, and no work may begin before signature.

Access and Data Handling
Vendor access to firm systems must be provisioned through AuthSSO with least privilege and a defined expiry. Shared credentials are prohibited. Vendors may receive only the minimum data needed for the service, and any vendor handling client records must store them in approved environments such as DocVault. Technology reviews vendor access lists every quarter.

Ongoing Monitoring
Tier 1 vendors are reviewed quarterly, Tier 2 vendors annually, and Tier 3 vendors every two years. Reviews cover service level performance, incidents, audit findings, financial condition, and changes in ownership or subcontractors. Results are reported to the Vendor Oversight Review, and material concerns are escalated to the CEO.

Incident Management
Any vendor-related outage, data exposure, or control failure must be reported in #incidents immediately and logged by the Business Owner. Technology leads technical triage, and Compliance determines whether regulatory notification is required. A post-incident review is required for every Tier 1 vendor incident.

Offboarding
When a relationship ends, the Business Owner coordinates revocation of all access within one business day, confirmation of data return or deletion, final invoice reconciliation with Finance, and updates to the vendor register and system dependency records.

Exceptions
Exceptions require written approval from the COO and the Head of Risk, with Compliance consulted where regulatory exposure exists. Exceptions expire after 90 days unless renewed.

Policy Review
This policy is reviewed annually by the COO and approved by the CEO. Questions should be directed to the COO's office.

title: Client Onboarding Checklist
text:
Client Onboarding Checklist
Owner: Sandra Stone, Client Associate, Wealth Management
Last updated: 2026-09-17

Purpose
This checklist covers the steps a Client Associate or Relationship Manager follows to take a new wealth management client from signed engagement to an active, funded relationship. It applies to individual, joint, trust and entity clients. Follow it in order. If a step cannot be completed, stop and escalate rather than skipping ahead.

Before You Start
Confirm the client's engagement letter has been countersigned by the Relationship Manager. Confirm you can sign in through AuthSSO, since DocVault and ClientHub both depend on it. If either application rejects your login, raise it in #it-ops before touching any client file.

Step 1: Create the Client Record
Open ClientHub and create the client profile. Enter the legal name, entity type, primary advisor and Relationship Manager exactly as they appear on the signed documents. Do not paste personal identifiers into free-text notes fields. Use the structured fields only. Assign the advisor team and tag the expected service tier.

Step 2: Collect Identity and Ownership Documents
Request the required documents using the standard request template. Individuals need government-issued photo ID and proof of address. Entities and trusts need formation documents, an ownership chart showing every beneficial owner at or above the firm threshold, and the authorized signer list. Upload everything to the client's folder in DocVault. Name files with the document type and date only, never the client's name or any account detail. Do not send documents by email or chat. If a client sends something that way, upload it to DocVault, then delete the message and let the client know.

Step 3: Submit to the KYC Pipeline
Once the ClientHub profile and DocVault folder are complete, submit the client to KYCPipeline. The pipeline pulls the profile from ClientHub, reads the documents from DocVault, and runs the name and ownership screening through SanctionsScreen. A submission will fail validation if the folder is missing a required document, so check the list in Step 2 first. Note that KYCPipeline ownership moves from Operations to Compliance on 2026-10-06. Until then, questions go to the KYC team contacts in Operations. After that date, send them to #kyc-pipeline and the Compliance KYC Specialists.

Step 4: Handle Screening Results
A clear result is recorded automatically. A potential match or an elevated risk rating routes the case to Compliance for review. Do not contact the client about a screening hit and do not discuss the reason with anyone outside Compliance. Wait for the KYC Specialist or the Senior AML Analyst to give you instructions. Cases involving politically exposed persons, high-risk jurisdictions or complex ownership require enhanced due diligence, which Compliance will request through the case record.

Step 5: Suitability and Account Documents
While screening runs, the advisor completes the risk profile and investment objectives questionnaire. The Portfolio Manager then drafts the proposed allocation. Account opening forms, fee schedule and disclosures must all be signed and stored in DocVault before any account is activated. Retain the signed copies. Do not rely on scanned photos that are cut off or unreadable.

Step 6: Approval and Activation
Activation requires three things: a cleared KYC status, a complete suitability file, and Relationship Manager sign-off in ClientHub. Only then ask Operations to open the account and set up funding instructions. Wire instructions must be verified with the client by a call-back to a known contact, never by replying to an email. Operations will not release the first funding until the call-back is logged.

Step 7: Closing the Loop
Send the welcome message through the approved template. Update ClientHub with the activation date and the next scheduled review. Add a reminder for the periodic KYC refresh according to the client's risk rating. Flag any open items to the advisor in #wealth-team without including client details.

Common Mistakes
Uploading documents to the wrong client folder. Entering personal identifiers in notes. Submitting before the ownership chart is final. Activating an account while a Compliance review is still open.

Questions
Process questions go to Sandra Stone. Screening and policy questions go to Compliance in #compliance. System access issues go to #it-ops.

title: AuthSSO Migration Plan
text:
Author: Priya Raman, Staff Engineer, Technology
Last updated: 2026-09-24
Status: Approved for execution, pending final sign-off from Sam Okafor

Purpose
This plan covers moving AuthSSO, our single sign-on and identity provider, from the current self-hosted deployment to the new managed identity platform. AuthSSO is a critical system with no upstream dependencies, but many services depend on it, so the migration is staged by dependent system rather than done as a single switch.

Scope and dependencies
Direct dependents of AuthSSO are OMS, ClientHub and DocVault. Indirect dependents are TradeBlotter (via OMS), SettlementEngine (via OMS), KYCPipeline (via ClientHub and DocVault), SARFiling (via DocVault) and LoanOrigination (via ClientHub and KYCPipeline). PricingSvc does not authenticate through AuthSSO, but OMS calls both, so every OMS verification step includes a pricing round trip to confirm order entry still works end to end.

Guiding principles
First, run old and new providers in parallel until each dependent is verified. Second, migrate lowest-risk systems first. Third, no critical system is cut over without a tested rollback of 15 minutes or less. Fourth, no cutover on a day with month-end or quarter-end settlement pressure.

Phases and dates
Phase 0, preparation (now through 2026-09-29): Leo Martinez finishes the token and claims mapping so group names, role claims and session lifetimes match the current provider. Omar Brown and Barbara Beard build the new health checks and alerting. Kevin Zhao completes the dual-validation shim that lets services accept tokens from either provider.

Phase 1, DocVault (2026-09-30): DocVault is a standard system with a small blast radius, so it goes first. Success criteria are document upload, retrieval and access-control checks passing for Compliance, Lending and Wealth Management test users. SARFiling and KYCPipeline both read from DocVault, so Compliance and Operations are told in advance and run a smoke test afterward.

Phase 2, ClientHub (2026-10-02): Grace Lin's team validates CRM logins and relationship-manager permissions. Lending checks that LoanOrigination can still resolve client records.

Phase 3, KYC ownership overlap (2026-10-06): KYCPipeline changes ownership from Operations to Compliance on this date. We make no AuthSSO changes to KYCPipeline that day. Jenna Cho and Marcus Bell confirm the service accounts are recorded under the Compliance owner group before any identity changes touch the pipeline.

Phase 4, OMS and downstream (target 2026-10-16, after market close): This is the highest-risk step. Daniel Reyes's desk must confirm that a test order can be entered, routed and shown in TradeBlotter. Ravi Patel's team confirms SettlementEngine picks up the test trade. If either check fails, we roll back to the old provider immediately. Leo Martinez runs the cutover and Vincent Green is backup.

Phase 5, decommission (week of 2026-10-26): Old provider stays in read-only standby for two weeks after Phase 4, then is retired once no authentication traffic hits it.

Rollback
The dual-validation shim remains enabled through Phase 4. Rollback means flipping the identity provider setting back to the old endpoint and restarting affected services, which has been rehearsed in staging at under 10 minutes. The incident channel is #incidents, and #it-ops carries the cutover status thread.

Risks
Session lifetime mismatches may log traders out mid-session. Mitigation is to match lifetimes exactly and schedule cutover after close. Group-claim gaps could lock out Compliance users from DocVault. Mitigation is a Compliance-led access test in Phase 1. Staffing is also a risk, since I leave the firm on 2026-10-09, one week before the OMS cutover.

Handoff
Before 2026-10-09 I will hand all runbooks, claim mappings and staging notes to Leo Martinez, who becomes plan owner. Vincent Green is secondary and Sam Okafor remains the approver. I will hold a walkthrough session for Technology, SRE and Operations on 2026-10-07 and update this document with final notes by 2026-10-08.

Open items
Confirm the OMS cutover window with Daniel Reyes. Confirm Ravi Patel's staffing for settlement verification. Add the Phase 4 go or no-go checklist to the runbook.

title: Data Classification Standard
text:
Data Classification Standard
Owner: Vincent Green, Senior Engineer, Technology
Last updated: 2026-09-24
Applies to: All Halcyon Ridge Capital employees, contractors, and systems

Purpose
This standard defines how Halcyon Ridge Capital classifies, labels, stores, and shares data. It gives every team a common vocabulary so that controls on our platforms match the sensitivity of the information they hold. It supports our obligations under securities, lending, and anti-money-laundering regulation and our duty to protect client and deal information.

Scope
The standard covers data in every production, staging, and analytics environment, including MarketDataFeed, PricingSvc, PositionStore, GLCore, DocVault, ClientHub, DataLake, and the systems that depend on them. It also covers email, Slack, shared drives, and exported reports.

Classification Levels
Public: Information approved for external release, such as published marketing material and press statements. No handling restrictions beyond brand review.

Internal: General business information not intended for outsiders, such as policies, org charts, runbooks, and non-sensitive Slack discussion in channels like #general and #it-ops. Default level for anything unlabeled that is not clearly higher.

Confidential: Information whose disclosure could harm clients or the firm. Examples include client records in ClientHub, onboarding files in KYCPipeline, loan files in LoanOrigination, credit models in CreditScoring, positions in PositionStore, risk outputs from RiskEngine, and trading strategies and P&L in TradeBlotter.

Restricted: The most sensitive information. Examples include material non-public information tied to M&A Advisory mandates (including anything discussed in #project-falcon), SAR content in SARFiling, sanctions and AML investigation material in SanctionsScreen and AMLMonitor, authentication secrets in AuthSSO, and wire instructions and payment credentials in PaymentsGateway and WireRoom. Existence of a SAR must never be disclosed outside the permitted Compliance workflow.

Data Owners and Custodians
Each system has an owner team, which is accountable for classifying its data. The owner team approves access requests and reviews entitlements quarterly. Technology acts as custodian for shared platforms such as DataLake and DocVault and is responsible for encryption, backup, and logging. Where ownership changes, the new owner inherits the classification duties from the effective date. For example, KYCPipeline moves from Operations to Compliance on 2026-10-06, and Compliance becomes the accountable owner from that date.

Handling Requirements
Internal: Store only on approved firm systems. Share within the firm freely.

Confidential: Access is role-based and granted through AuthSSO groups. Data must be encrypted in transit and at rest. Share only with people who have a business need. Slack discussion belongs in channels appropriate to the audience, and raw data should not be pasted into public channels. Exports from ReportingBI or DataLake require a documented purpose.

Restricted: Access is named-individual, approved by the data owner and by Compliance, and reviewed monthly. Wall-crossed lists govern deal data, and Compliance maintains them. Restricted data may not be copied to personal devices, personal email, or unapproved cloud storage. It must not be used in non-production environments unless masked or tokenized. Transfers require encrypted channels and are logged.

Labeling
Documents in DocVault carry a classification label in their metadata. Reports in ReportingBI display the level in the header. Datasets in DataLake are tagged at the table and column level by the owning team, and the highest classification of any column determines the table level. Derived data inherits the highest classification of its inputs unless the owner documents a downgrade after review.

Non-Production Use
Production Confidential and Restricted data must not be loaded into development or test environments. Engineers should use synthetic or masked data sets. Any exception requires written approval from the data owner and the Chief Compliance Officer, and a defined expiry date.

Retention and Disposal
Retention follows the firm records schedule maintained by Compliance. When retention expires, data is deleted from primary stores, DataLake copies, and backups according to the schedule. Disposal of Restricted data is logged and verified by Technology.

Incident Reporting
Suspected misclassification, mis-sharing, or exposure of Confidential or Restricted data must be reported immediately in #incidents or directly to Compliance. Do not delete evidence. Compliance and Technology will assess whether regulatory or client notification is required.

Exceptions and Review
Exceptions are requested through the data owner and approved by the Chief Compliance Officer. This standard is reviewed annually, or sooner after a significant system or ownership change. Questions can be sent to Vincent Green or raised in #it-ops.

title: Business Continuity Plan: WireRoom and LoanOrigination
text:
Business Continuity Plan: WireRoom and LoanOrigination
Author: Kevin Zhao, Software Engineer, Technology
Last updated: 2026-09-25
Status: Working draft for review by Operations, Lending, Compliance and Risk

Purpose and Scope
This plan describes how Halcyon Ridge Capital keeps wire transfer operations and loan origination running, or restores them quickly, during a technology outage or loss of staff or facilities. It covers WireRoom (the wire transfer operations console) and LoanOrigination (the loan origination system) and the upstream services they depend on. It does not replace the firm-wide plan owned by Linda Brandt, COO.

Dependency Map
WireRoom depends on PaymentsGateway. PaymentsGateway depends on GLCore and FraudScore, and FraudScore depends on DataLake. An outage in any of these affects wire release even when the WireRoom console itself is healthy.

LoanOrigination depends on ClientHub, CreditScoring and KYCPipeline. ClientHub depends on AuthSSO. KYCPipeline depends on ClientHub, DocVault and SanctionsScreen. CreditScoring depends on DataLake. An AuthSSO failure therefore blocks loan intake as well as wire entry.

Recovery Priorities
Tier 1 (restore first): AuthSSO, GLCore, PaymentsGateway, FraudScore, SanctionsScreen. Target recovery is 2 hours.
Tier 2: WireRoom, KYCPipeline, ClientHub, DocVault. Target recovery is 4 hours.
Tier 3: LoanOrigination, CreditScoring, DataLake. Target recovery is 8 hours.
Only Tier 1 and Tier 2 items are treated as same-day critical for the wire function. Loan closings can usually slip a business day without regulatory impact.

WireRoom Continuity Procedures
If WireRoom is unavailable but PaymentsGateway is healthy, Ravi Patel, Head of Operations, may authorize wire room specialists to submit instructions directly through the PaymentsGateway administrative interface. Every manually keyed wire requires dual approval by two wire room specialists and a callback verification where the client's standing instructions require it.

If FraudScore is degraded, wires are not released on a bypass. Marcus Bell, Chief Compliance Officer, or his delegate decides whether to hold all outbound wires or to allow low-value releases after manual screening by the AML team led by Nadia Petrov. Sanctions screening through SanctionsScreen is never skipped.

If GLCore is unavailable, wires are queued and not released, because posting must be possible. Operations logs queued items in the shared outage tracker and reconciles them against GLCore once it is restored. The #recon channel is used to flag any breaks that follow.

LoanOrigination Continuity Procedures
If LoanOrigination is down, Brian Kowalski, Head of Lending, activates the offline pipeline. Loan officers record new applications on the approved intake template stored in DocVault. Senior underwriters Joshua Gordon and Tammy Murphy continue credit review using the last exported pipeline report and CreditScoring outputs. Loan closers, led by Brandon George, hold all funding until the system is restored and the file has been reconciled.

If KYCPipeline is degraded, no loan may be funded without a completed KYC and CDD decision. Compliance KYC specialists may complete reviews manually and record outcomes in the #kyc-pipeline channel until the pipeline returns.

Ownership Change Note
Ownership of KYCPipeline moves from Operations to Compliance on 2026-10-06. Until that date, Operations is the escalation contact for KYCPipeline incidents. After that date, Compliance is the escalation contact, and this plan, the on-call rota and the contact sheet will be updated to reflect it. Jenna Cho, Compliance Engineering Lead, is the technical point of contact for the transition.

Staffing and Knowledge Risk
Priya Raman, Staff Engineer, leaves the firm on 2026-10-09. Her runbooks for the AuthSSO failover and DataLake restore must be reviewed and handed to Leo Martinez and Vincent Green before that date. Sam Okafor, Director of Engineering, owns that handoff. Omar Brown and Barbara Beard, Site Reliability Engineers, are the primary on-call contacts for infrastructure recovery.

Communication
Declare incidents in #incidents with the affected systems and a severity. Operations and Lending leads post updates at least every 60 minutes during a Tier 1 event. Wealth Management and Trading are notified through their channel leads if client payments are delayed. Catherine Hale, CEO, is informed of any outage lasting longer than 4 hours or involving a regulatory reporting obligation.

Testing and Review
Technology, Operations and Lending run a tabletop exercise each quarter covering a combined AuthSSO and PaymentsGateway outage. Failover of the offline loan intake process is tested twice a year. Findings go to Owen Gallagher, Head of Risk, and this plan is revised after each test and after any Tier 1 incident.

title: Incident Management Process
text:
Incident Management Process
Owner: Technology (Site Reliability Engineering)
Author: Angelica Schneider, Senior Engineer
Last updated: 2026-09-29

Purpose and Scope
This procedure defines how Halcyon Ridge Capital detects, declares, manages, and reviews production incidents affecting any firm system, from MarketDataFeed and OMS through to HRIS. It applies to Technology, Trading, Wealth Management, Lending, M&A Advisory, Compliance, Risk, and Operations staff. Security incidents and suspected data exposure follow this process but are also escalated to Compliance as described below.

Severity Levels
Sev1: A critical system is down or materially degraded, or there is regulatory, financial, or market impact. Examples: OMS unavailable during market hours, PaymentsGateway failing wires, AuthSSO outage, SanctionsScreen or AMLMonitor not processing.
Sev2: A critical system is partially degraded with a workaround, or a standard system is down for a business-critical function. Examples: ReportingBI stale before a regulatory deadline, PortfolioMgr rebalancing failures.
Sev3: Limited impact on a standard or legacy system, no immediate business deadline at risk. Example: a failed ReconLegacy batch with time to rerun.
Sev4: Cosmetic or low-impact issue, handled through the normal ticket queue.
When in doubt, declare higher and downgrade later.

Roles
Incident Commander (IC): Runs the response, assigns work, and decides on severity changes. For Sev1 and Sev2 the IC is the on-call SRE (Omar Brown or Barbara Beard in the current rotation) unless the Director of Engineering, Sam Okafor, takes over.
Technical Lead: The engineer from the owning team of the affected system.
Communications Lead: Posts updates and keeps stakeholders informed. Defaults to the IC for Sev2 and below, and to a delegate named by the IC for Sev1.
Business Liaison: A representative from the impacted desk or function, such as Daniel Reyes for Trading, Ravi Patel for Operations, Grace Lin for Wealth Management, or Brian Kowalski for Lending.

Detection and Declaration
Incidents are detected by monitoring alerts, user reports, or vendor notices. Anyone can declare an incident. Post in #incidents with the affected system, observed symptoms, start time, and your best severity estimate. The on-call SRE acknowledges within 10 minutes for Sev1 and 30 minutes for Sev2, opens a ticket, and names the IC in the thread. Use #it-ops for general technology questions, and keep #incidents reserved for active incidents and status updates.

Dependency-Aware Triage
Before chasing symptoms, check upstream systems. Many incidents are downstream effects of a single root cause.
- MarketDataFeed problems surface in PricingSvc, then in RiskEngine, OMS, TradeBlotter, and PortfolioMgr.
- AuthSSO problems affect OMS, ClientHub, and DocVault, and indirectly KYCPipeline, SARFiling, and LoanOrigination.
- DataLake problems affect FraudScore, AMLMonitor, CreditScoring, and ReportingBI.
- GLCore problems affect SettlementEngine, PaymentsGateway, ReconLegacy, and ReportingBI.
The IC should open one parent incident and link downstream alerts to it rather than running parallel incidents.

Response Steps
1. Stabilize: Prefer rollback, failover, or feature flag over a forward fix during an active Sev1 or Sev2.
2. Keep a timeline in the incident thread, noting every action with a timestamp.
3. Freeze non-essential deployments to affected systems and their dependencies until the IC lifts the freeze.
4. Use the weekly-published runbook for the system if one exists. ReconLegacy runs on Perl and Oracle 11g and is best-effort only, so engage its Technology owner early and coordinate reruns with Operations in #recon.

Communication Cadence
Sev1: Update in #incidents every 30 minutes, with a note to the Executive Office (Linda Brandt as COO) at declaration and at resolution. Sev2: Update every 60 minutes. Sev3: Update at start and resolution. Updates state impact, current theory, next step, and next update time. Do not speculate on causes in broad channels.

Compliance and Risk Escalation
Notify Compliance (Marcus Bell) immediately if an incident touches SanctionsScreen, AMLMonitor, FraudScore, KYCPipeline, or SARFiling, or involves possible unauthorized access to client records in DocVault or ClientHub. Notify Risk (Owen Gallagher) if RiskEngine or market data used for exposure calculations is degraded, so that manual limit monitoring can start. Any gap in screening or monitoring must be documented so Compliance can assess regulatory reporting obligations.

Ownership Change Notice
KYCPipeline moves from Operations to Compliance ownership on 2026-10-06. Until then, KYCPipeline incidents are led by Operations. From that date, Compliance is the owning team and supplies the Technical Lead, with Technology supporting. Runbooks and the on-call escalation list will be updated on the same date.

Resolution and Post-Incident Review
The IC closes the incident once service is verified healthy by the owning team and the business liaison. A blameless post-incident review is required within five business days for Sev1 and Sev2. It covers the timeline, root cause, detection gaps, what went well, and action items with owners and due dates. Reviews are filed in the engineering wiki and summarized in #incidents. Action items are tracked as tickets and reviewed monthly by Sam Okafor and Linda Brandt.

Document Maintenance
This procedure is reviewed quarterly. Send suggested changes to Angelica Schneider or post them in #it-ops.

title: PaymentsGateway Runbook
text:
PaymentsGateway Runbook
Owner: Operations (Ravi Patel, Head of Operations)
Last updated: 2026-09-30
Criticality: Critical

Purpose
This runbook covers day-to-day operation, monitoring, and incident response for PaymentsGateway, the ACH and wire payments gateway.
